p: Welcome to the first lesson of the course. In this lesson we go back to the very beginning of every spirit: the field, the orchard, the fermenting vat. We look at the four stages of production, at what a raw material really gives the distiller, at how starch and inulin are turned into sugar, and at what happens when yeast gets to work. These ideas may sound basic, but every later lesson, from Cognac to Scotch, is built on them.

First, the big picture. Every spirit, from the humblest to the most prestigious, goes through four stages. A raw material is chosen and processed to obtain a sugary liquid. That liquid is fermented and becomes alcoholic. It is then distilled, to concentrate the alcohol and the aromas the producer wants to keep. Finally come the operations after distillation, such as maturing, blending and preparing the spirit for the bottle. At each stage the producer makes choices, and every choice leaves its mark on style and quality.

Sometimes those choices are free, and sometimes the law decides. For certain spirits the rules fix the raw material, the type of still or the minimum time in oak. Think of a recipe handed down in a family: some cooks improvise, while others must follow the instructions to the letter if they want to keep the dish's traditional name. In the coming lessons you will meet many of these legal recipes, so keep this idea in mind.

Now, the raw material. In principle a spirit can be made from any farm product that contains carbohydrates: grapes, apples, grains, sugar cane, potatoes or agave. The raw material gives the distiller two things. The first is a store of carbohydrate, which is the food that yeast will turn into alcohol. No carbohydrate, no fermentation, and so nothing to distil. The second gift is flavour, and here we need a new word.

That word is congeners. Congeners are all the compounds, other than ethanol and water, that give a spirit its aroma and taste. Some come straight from the raw material. Every Tequila, for example, shares earthy, peppery notes that come from blue agave, whatever else the producer does. Vodka is the great exception: its producers strip out almost all the congeners, so the character of the raw material nearly vanishes. And because distillation concentrates everything, quality matters from the start. Picture reducing a sauce: if one ingredient was slightly off, the fault only grows stronger. A small flaw in the raw material can become a glaring one in the glass.

Next, the problem of starch. Yeast can only feed on simple sugars. Grapes and sugar cane already contain them, so the juice simply has to be extracted. But grains and potatoes store their energy as starch, and the heart of the agave stores it as inulin. Both are complex carbohydrates, far too large for yeast to eat. Before fermentation, they must be broken down into sugar. There are three main ways to do it.

The first way uses the plant's own chemistry, and it is called malting. Barley grains are dampened and kept warm until they begin to sprout. The young plant releases enzymes, natural substances that can cut starch into sugar. After a few days the grains are heated to stop the growth. The second way is cooking: other grains, such as corn, rye and wheat, are crushed and cooked in water, which makes the starch soluble, and then a little malted barley is added so that its enzymes can do the conversion.

Potatoes follow a similar path: they are cooked until they break down into a cloudy, starchy liquid, and then bought-in enzymes are added. Many grain distillers also use these ready-made enzymes. The third way is heat alone, and it belongs to agave. The heart of the plant, called the piña, is cooked, which turns its inulin into sugars, and is then crushed to release a sweet juice. So remember the pairs: starch for grains and potatoes, inulin for agave.

Now, fermentation. Once the producer has a sugary liquid, yeast is added. The yeast eats the sugar and produces three things: alcohol, carbon dioxide and congeners. The carbon dioxide is a waste gas; it bubbles up so vigorously that the vat can look as if it were boiling. The alcohol and the congeners, on the other hand, are exactly what the distiller will later work with.

What does the liquid contain at the end? Mostly water and alcohols. By far the most important alcohol is ethanol, but there are others too, such as methanol and the so-called fusel alcohols. Fermentation stops once all the sugar is used up, and producers usually aim for a liquid of about eight to ten percent alcohol by volume, roughly the strength of a sturdy beer. A word on measures: in the United States strength is often given in proof, and two degrees of proof equal one percent alcohol by volume. So a spirit at forty percent can be labelled eighty proof.

Fermentation is also a flavour factory. Many congeners are born here, and one group is especially important: the esters, which smell fruity. And here is the key point of the whole lesson. Distillation creates nothing new; it can only select and concentrate what is already in the liquid. If an aroma is missing after fermentation, it will never appear in the spirit. That is why almost every producer uses selected yeast that behaves the same way every time, batch after batch.

Here is a memory tip. Think of the raw material as the ingredients, fermentation as the cooking, and distillation as the reduction of the sauce. Reduction makes the flavours stronger, but it cannot add a taste that was never in the pan. So whenever you wonder where an aroma in a spirit comes from, start by asking two questions: was it in the raw material, or was it created by the yeast?

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, every spirit passes through four stages, and the raw material provides both carbohydrates for the yeast and congeners for flavour. Second, starch in grains and potatoes, and inulin in agave, must become sugar first, through malting, cooking with enzymes, or cooking alone in the case of agave. Third, yeast turns sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and congeners, reaching about eight to ten percent, and distillation can only concentrate what fermentation has created.

In this lesson we step into the still house. Before we look at real stills, we need to understand what distillation is trying to do, and the simple physics that makes it possible. We will see why distillation is about choosing as much as concentrating, how a distiller separates the liquid into heads, heart, tails and waste, and why the strength a spirit reaches decides how much aroma it keeps. Get this lesson right, and the next two, on pot and column stills, will fall neatly into place.

Let's start with the purpose. Distillation picks out some parts of the fermented liquid and leaves the rest behind. The result is concentration. The most obvious part to concentrate is ethanol: a liquid of about ten percent alcohol by volume often becomes a spirit of about seventy-five percent. Some spirits are collected at a lower strength than that, while others climb as high as ninety-six percent. That is the ceiling, and you will see why it matters.

But alcohol is only half the story. Distillation is also about choosing which congeners to keep, in other words which aromas will carry the spirit's character. The distiller decides according to personal taste and the style of product. A spirit meant to be full of personality needs plenty of congeners; a spirit meant to be almost neutral needs very few. Think of a photographer framing a picture: what is left outside the frame matters as much as what stays in.

All newly made spirits share two features. They come off the still colourless, as clear as water, and they are dry, which means they contain no sugar. So where do the amber colour of an old brandy and the gentle sweetness of some rums come from? Not from the still. They arrive later, from oak or from additions made after distillation. If you taste a spirit straight from the still, you find only alcohol and aromas.

Now the physics. Pure ethanol boils at about seventy-eight degrees Celsius, while water boils at one hundred. We say that ethanol is more volatile. So when a mixture of water and alcohol is heated to boiling, the vapour that rises contains a higher proportion of ethanol than the liquid it came from. Collect that vapour, cool it in a condenser, and it turns back into a liquid, but a stronger one. Heat, condense, collect: that is the whole principle.

Real life is a little messier. A fermented liquid is not just water and ethanol; it holds hundreds of different components, called fractions, each with its own boiling point. To keep things manageable, distillers think of them in four groups. First, congeners that boil before ethanol, the most volatile of all. Second, ethanol together with the congeners that boil at a similar temperature. Third, congeners that boil after ethanol. And fourth, water.

Those four groups match the four parts a distiller separates. The heads are the most volatile compounds, and they smell of solvent, a bit like nail-polish remover. The heart contains the ethanol and the aromas that give the spirit its character: this is the part that will be sold. The tails come last, and they bring heavy notes that recall cheese or plastic. What remains at the end, mostly water, is the liquid waste. The moment when the distiller switches from collecting one part to the next is called a cut.

Notice a subtle point. Heads and tails are not entirely bad. They contain unwanted congeners, but also a good deal of ethanol and some of the pleasant aromas, so they are rarely simply thrown away. That is why the position of the cuts is such a personal decision. A generous heart keeps more of these borderline compounds and gives a richer, more intense spirit; a narrow heart gives a cleaner, more delicate one. We will see how each type of still handles them.

Now the golden rule of this lesson. The higher the strength a spirit is distilled to, the fewer aromas it keeps. As the concentration of ethanol rises, more and more congeners are left behind. Picture a sieve that keeps getting finer: in the end almost only alcohol slips through, and the scent of the raw material stays outside. This is not a matter of opinion; it is the chemistry of separation.

Let's put numbers on it. A spirit collected at around seventy-five percent keeps plenty of congeners and has a medium or pronounced aroma intensity. At around ninety percent the aroma becomes light, as in some light rums or in Scottish grain whisky. At ninety-five or ninety-six percent so few congeners remain that the spirit is called neutral. Neutral spirit is the starting point for vodka, and for many gins and liqueurs that take their flavour from elsewhere.

This single choice explains a great deal of the difference between spirits. A vodka made from neutral spirit barely recalls its raw material. An Armagnac or a Bourbon, collected at a much lower strength, keeps the grape or the corn clearly in view. So when you meet a new spirit, ask first how strong it was when it left the still. As we will see in the next lessons, the type of still matters, but the strength reached matters even more.

Here is a memory tip. Imagine a radio in a crowded room. The aromas are the music, the alcohol is the noise of the crowd. At seventy-five percent the music is clear; at ninety, you can just hear the tune; at ninety-six the crowd drowns it out completely. The louder the alcohol, the fainter the music.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, distillation selects and concentrates: it raises the alcohol, typically from about ten to about seventy-five percent, and chooses which congeners to keep, giving a spirit that is colourless and dry. Second, because ethanol is more volatile than water, the distiller can separate heads with their solvent smell, a heart full of character, tails with cheesy or plastic notes, and watery waste. Third, the higher the distillation strength, the less aroma remains: medium to pronounced around seventy-five, light around ninety, neutral at ninety-five or ninety-six.

In this lesson we take a close look at the oldest and most iconic piece of equipment in any distillery: the pot still. We will walk through its parts, from the heat source to the condenser, then follow the two distillations that turn a fermented liquid into a spirit. We will see why the heads and tails are kept and sent round again, and why a pot still gives a spirit full of aroma. By the end you should be able to picture every step, as if you were standing beside the distiller.

First, the look of the thing. A pot still resembles a giant copper kettle, and copper is no accident: it is easy to shape and it conducts heat very well. At the bottom is the heat source. Today it is nearly always steam, running through coils inside the pot or through a jacket around it. Direct fire, with flames under the pot, has become rare, although Cognac still uses it because the law requires it, typically with gas burners.

Now let's follow the path of the vapour. The pot holds the liquid to be distilled, and a drain at the bottom lets the distiller empty it at the end of each run. Above the pot rises the still head, where the vapours gather. It narrows into the swan neck, a graceful curve that leads into a pipe called the lyne arm, which carries the vapours across to the condenser. So the route is: pot, still head, swan neck, lyne arm, condenser. Say it a few times; the exam likes it.

The condenser is where vapour becomes liquid again. Inside, the hot vapours meet pipes filled with a cold coolant, usually water, and they condense into the newly made spirit. The most common design today is the shell and tube condenser. There is also an older design, a long coiled pipe sitting in a tank of cold water, called a worm tub. Whatever the design, the cooling water must be constantly renewed, otherwise it warms up and stops doing its job.

A pot still works in batches. You fill it, distil, empty it, clean it and start again, much like a washing machine. And one run is never enough: at least two distillations are needed. In the first, the pot is filled with the fermented liquid at around ten percent alcohol and brought to the boil. The aim here is simple: get rid of a large part of the water. Everything that comes off the condenser is collected for several hours, until the flow is down to about one percent alcohol. The watery residue left in the pot is thrown away.

The liquid collected from this first run is called low wines, and it is only twenty-five to thirty percent alcohol. Why so weak? Because the pot runs out of alcohol as it boils, so the strength of the flow keeps falling. To recover all the alcohol and all the good aromas, the distiller has to keep collecting until the very end, and that means collecting a lot of water too. The low wines are a halfway house, not yet a spirit.

The second distillation creates a liquid that can be sold, and this is where the cuts come in. The pot is filled with the low wines and heated again. First come the heads, with their sharp solvent smell, for about ten to fifteen minutes. When that smell fades, the distiller makes the first cut, sending the flow to a different tank: this is the heart. Its strength falls steadily as the run goes on, and the heart collected overall ends up at about seventy-five percent alcohol.

When cheesy or plastic notes start to appear, the distiller makes a second cut, and the flow becomes the tails. Here is a detail worth remembering: the tails go into the same tank as the heads. They are collected until the flow drops to about one percent alcohol, then the still is shut down and the watery residue in the pot is discarded. So after each second distillation, the distiller has two things: a tank of heart, and a tank of heads and tails mixed together.

Why keep the heads and tails? Because, as we saw in the last lesson, they contain unwanted congeners but also plenty of ethanol and some positive aromas. Throwing them away would waste both alcohol and character. So in the next cycle, the pot for the second distillation is filled with the new batch of low wines plus the heads and tails from the previous run. It is like a cook keeping leftover stock for tomorrow's soup: nothing good is wasted, and the house style carries over from one batch to the next.

Where exactly the cuts fall is a matter of the distiller's taste and the type of spirit. A wider cut lets more of the borderline compounds into the heart and gives a more intense, more robust spirit. A narrower cut gives a cleaner, more delicate one. Two distilleries working with identical pot stills and identical low wines can therefore produce rather different spirits, simply by moving the cuts a few minutes earlier or later.

So what kind of spirit comes out of a pot still? The separation in the second distillation is not very precise. Along with the ethanol, many congeners with a similar boiling point slip into the heart, and they give the spirit its personality. The typical result has a medium to pronounced aroma intensity. There is also a physical limit: because every batch must be fully recovered, water comes along too, and the strength can never climb to ninety-six percent. You simply cannot make neutral spirit with a double distillation in a pot still.

The price of all this character is work. Each batch has to be loaded, heated, watched, cut and emptied, and then the whole cycle begins again. Producers who choose pot stills rarely do so to make huge volumes quickly. They choose them to make expressive spirits, in which you can still recognise the raw material and the fermentation behind it.

Here is a memory tip. Think of the low wines as a rough draft and the second distillation as the final edit. In the edit, the heads are the clumsy opening lines and the tails the rambling ending; both are cut, but they go back in the drawer, because a few good sentences can be reused in the next draft.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, the vapour travels from the pot through the still head, swan neck and lyne arm into the condenser, which may be a shell and tube design or an old-fashioned worm tub. Second, the first distillation gives low wines at twenty-five to thirty percent, and the second is cut into heads, a heart of about seventy-five percent, and tails, with heads and tails added to the next batch. Third, a pot still works in batches, cannot reach ninety-six percent, and gives spirits with medium to pronounced aromas.

In the last lesson we watched a pot still work, one batch at a time. Now we turn to its tall, tireless partner: the column still. In this lesson we look inside the column, at its plates, bubble caps and downcomers, and at how it is heated. Then we see how many distillations can happen at once in a still that never needs to stop, and finally why a column can make almost any style of spirit, from completely neutral to richly flavoured.

Let's open the door. A column still is a tall tower divided inside by many horizontal plates, stacked one above the other. On each plate sits a layer of boiling alcoholic liquid. Small porthole windows in the side let the distiller look in and check what is happening on each plate. Designs vary enormously, but they all work on the same principles. Think of a block of flats where every floor has the same layout and does the same job.

Now the clever part: how a plate works. Each plate has a hole in it, and over the hole sits a bubble cap. Vapour rising from the plate below passes up through the hole, but the cap forces it to turn and bubble through the liquid sitting on the plate. That hot vapour keeps the liquid boiling, and the new vapour that rises from it is richer in the more volatile fractions. It climbs to the next plate up, and the process repeats.

What about the liquid? As vapour condenses on each plate, the level of liquid rises. When the plate is full, the extra liquid overflows down a pipe called the downcomer, onto the plate below. So inside the column there are two constant movements: vapour going up through the bubble caps, and liquid running down through the downcomers. Picture a busy staircase with people going up on one side and down on the other, never colliding.

How is it heated? Column stills normally use steam rather than a flame. A common method is a heat exchanger: boiling liquid from the base of the still circulates through pipes outside the column, and those pipes are heated by high-pressure steam. The heat passes through the metal, but the steam and the alcoholic liquid never touch. In some larger stills, steam is instead injected directly into the base of the column.

Here is the key idea of this lesson. A small distillation takes place on every single plate, and all of them happen at the same time. Each plate concentrates the volatile fractions a little more than the one below it. A column with dozens of plates is, in effect, dozens of distillations stacked on top of each other, running simultaneously. That is why a column can separate the fractions so much more precisely than a pot still.

And it never needs to stop. Fermented liquid is fed in continuously at the base, pre-heated almost to boiling, since the base is the hottest part and its heat powers everything above. Heads leave in a steady stream near the top, usually from a plate just below it. Tails are drawn off continuously from one of the lower plates. Watery waste leaves from the base. As long as the volume going in equals the volume coming out, the still is said to be in balance, and it can run without a break. In practice it is shut down from time to time for cleaning.

This continuous flow also explains why a column can reach strengths a pot still never can. In a pot still, each batch must be recovered completely, so water always comes along with the alcohol. In a column, ethanol keeps rising and water keeps falling, and nothing has to be emptied out before the next round. With enough plates, the spirit can reach ninety-six percent alcohol by volume. Only a column still can do that.

Now let's follow the congeners. Each one rises from plate to plate until it reaches the plate where it is the least volatile compound around. Above that point, its concentration drops away quickly. So the fractions spread out over the height of the tower in neat layers, like sediment settling in a jar. In theory, in a column with forty plates, the distiller can choose which plate to draw the heart from, and that choice sets the style.

Draw the heart from a plate at about seventy-five percent and it still holds plenty of congeners, with a medium or pronounced intensity, very much like a pot-still spirit at the same strength. Armagnac, Bourbon and rhum agricole are made this way: column stills, yet full of character. Climb higher, and more congeners are left behind. At about ninety percent the aroma is light, as in light rums and Scottish grain whisky. At ninety-five or ninety-six percent so few congeners remain that the spirit is neutral.

That level is even fixed by law. In the United States a neutral spirit must be distilled to at least ninety-five percent, and in the European Union to at least ninety-six. So the next time someone tells you that a column still always makes a light or neutral spirit, you can correct them politely. The column is a flexible tool: what matters is where the heart is drawn off and the strength it reaches.

Here is a memory tip. Think of the column as a tall apartment building where each family of aromas lives on its own floor. The heavy, earthy families live near the ground; the light, volatile ones at the top. The distiller is the visitor who decides which floor to call on. Stop on a low floor and you meet a crowd of characters; ride the lift to the top and the corridor is almost empty.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, a column is divided into many plates; bubble caps force the rising vapour through the liquid on each plate, downcomers carry the overflow down, and heat usually comes from steam, often through a heat exchanger. Second, a distillation happens on every plate at the same time, so the column runs continuously, with heads near the top, tails from a low plate and waste from the base, and only a column can reach ninety-six percent. Third, the style depends on where the heart is taken: medium to pronounced around seventy-five, light around ninety, neutral at ninety-five or ninety-six.

The spirit has left the still: colourless, dry and usually far too strong to drink. In this lesson we follow what happens next. There are four groups of operations, normally in this order: maturation, adding other flavours, blending, and finishing before bottling. Not every spirit goes through all four; it depends on the law and on the producer's choices. We will see what oak really does, what inert vessels are for, how flavours are added, why blending matters, and how a spirit is prepared for the bottle.

First choice: where does the spirit rest? Either in an oak barrel or in an inert vessel. Oak changes a spirit in several ways at once. It adds colour, from pale lemon to gold, and a whole range of congeners straight from the wood, with aromas such as vanilla, coconut, cinnamon and clove. Over the years, oxygen seeps in through the wood and reacts with the spirit, creating notes of leather and mushroom that are known as rancio, while the colour deepens towards amber and finally brown.

Oak also concentrates. Every year some water and alcohol evaporate through the wood, and this loss is called the angels' share. With very old spirits a barrel can lose more than half its contents, but what remains is far more intense and complex. And oak smooths. The inside of a barrel is charred or toasted when it is made, and that layer of carbon captures some of the harsh congeners of a young spirit. So oak gives, oxidises, concentrates and polishes.

The producer then has three key choices. The first is the barrel's age. A brand-new barrel gives the most colour and flavour, and each refill gives less. That does not make old barrels inferior; it depends on the style wanted. The second is the barrel's previous contents. Some liquid always stays soaked in the wood, and it comes back out into the next spirit, adding its own flavour. The third is warehouse temperature, and it deserves a closer look.

To pick up colour and flavour, the spirit has to move in and out of the wooden staves, and heat speeds this up. A Bourbon maturing through scorching Kentucky summers reaches maturity sooner, and with a deeper colour, than a Scotch resting in cool Scotland. Even inside one warehouse, the top is warmer than the bottom, and clever producers use that variation when they build their blends. One more point: because so much flavour comes from the wood, poor-quality barrels can ruin an excellent spirit.

When the effect of oak is not wanted, inert vessels are used, usually stainless steel or glass. They add no colour and no flavour, so the spirit stays water-white. Most spirits stored this way rest only briefly and change very little: they are described as unaged. But if they are left for several months or years, they become smoother and more mouth-filling, while staying colourless. And some very old oak-aged spirits, notably Cognac, are moved into glass demijohns to stop further oxidation and evaporation, preserving them at their peak.

The second group of operations is adding other flavours, mainly for flavoured spirits and liqueurs. The simplest method is maceration: fruit or botanicals, meaning herbs and spices, are steeped in alcohol, usually diluted with water, because very strong alcohol would extract harsh flavours. It can last from hours to months, sometimes with gentle heat. The result, sometimes called a tincture, carries colour and a full range of flavours, but the method cannot single out particular aromas.

That is the job of redistillation. Diluted neutral spirit is put in a pot still with the botanicals, sometimes after a short maceration, and distilled again. The aromas come off in order of volatility, and the distiller collects the heart while the wanted aromas are arriving. The result is sometimes called a distillate. For delicate botanicals such as cucumber, which would be spoiled by normal temperatures, a vacuum still lets the liquid boil at a lower temperature. The third method is simply buying flavourings, natural or artificial, and blending them in; this is sometimes called cold compounding.

The third group is blending, and the vast majority of spirits on sale are blends of spirits of different ages, or spirits distilled or matured in different ways. The blender has two aims. The first is consistency: buyers expect every bottle to taste the same, and this is especially hard with oak-aged spirits, because two barrels side by side can be strikingly different. Mixing many barrels evens out those differences.

The second aim is complexity. A very old spirit can be so intense that it lacks balance, while a young one may lack depth. Add a little of the old spirit to the young one and you get a harmony neither has on its own. There is no fixed recipe, because components change and run out over the years, so blenders need the widest possible palette. Think of a conductor who must make the orchestra sound the same every night, even when some musicians change.

Finally, finishing. Hardly any spirit is bottled exactly as it comes out of the cask or tank. First, water: almost every spirit is reduced to selling strength with completely pure water. Undiluted bottlings exist but are rare. Next, colour: tiny amounts of caramel, a tasteless food colouring, make batches of an oak-aged spirit look identical. Then sweetness: since all spirits start out dry, sugar may be added, for style in some brandies and rums, and by law in liqueurs.

Last comes filtration, to keep the spirit bright and clear right into the glass. A spirit can turn hazy when chilled, so in chill-filtration it is cooled, the haze is allowed to form, and then it is filtered out. Activated charcoal is a much finer filter that strips out congeners and colour; it is used for some white rums and for vodka. Producers who skip filtration often say so on the label, with words such as unfiltered or non-chill-filtered.

Here is a memory tip: think of a tailor. The still delivers the fabric; maturation dyes and softens it; added flavours are the embroidery; blending sews the pieces together; and finishing is the final pressing before the suit goes in the window. And not every suit gets every step: an unaged spirit skips the dye, and most spirits skip the embroidery.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, oak adds colour and flavour, creates rancio through oxygen, concentrates through the angels' share and removes harshness, shaped by barrel age, previous contents and warehouse temperature, while inert vessels of steel or glass leave the spirit colourless. Second, flavours can be added by maceration, by redistillation, sometimes in a vacuum still, or with bought-in flavourings, and blending aims at consistency and complexity. Third, finishing means pure water, possibly caramel and sugar, and filtration by chilling or with activated charcoal.

Welcome to the world's great fruit spirits. In this lesson we start with how fruit is turned into a spirit, from grapes, apples and pears to pomace, the skins winemakers leave behind. Then we visit the two most famous grape brandies of France: Cognac and Armagnac. They share a grape and a country, yet they are made in strikingly different ways, and the exam loves to compare them.

First, the fruit itself. Any fruit can be distilled, and almost every fruit-growing region has its own spirit. What all fruit has in common is urgency. Once picked, fruit starts to deteriorate and soon develops off-aromas that would end up in the glass. That is why distilleries work with fruit grown close by and process it quickly. Most fruit is crushed and pressed, the sweet juice is fermented, and the result is distilled. Apples and pears follow this route too.

When it comes to grapes, distillers have a surprising preference: white grapes with high acidity and little aroma. They make rather plain wine, but distillation concentrates their delicate floral and fruity notes. The grapes are pressed, the skins and seeds are set aside, and the juice ferments into wine. Since there is only one harvest a year, that wine must wait its turn in the distillery. Acidity and alcohol protect it for a while, but not for ever, so it has to be distilled within a few months. Pisco, which we meet in the next lesson, takes the opposite path with highly aromatic grapes.

Now, pomace. It is processed in two different ways, depending on the colour of the grape. White grape skins are pressed off before fermentation, still moist with juice, so the distiller mixes them with water and ferments that liquid. Black grape skins, on the other hand, ferment together with the juice to give red wine its colour, so they arrive at the distillery already soaked in alcohol and can be distilled straight away. Pomace brings herbaceous, spicy notes, quite unlike a brandy made from the wine itself.

A few more general points. Some fruits are not fermented at all: they are steeped in neutral spirit and then redistilled, either because they give too little juice or to avoid fermentation aromas. Most top-quality fruit spirits come from pot stills, although columns are used too. And as a rule, grape and apple brandies are matured in oak, while pomace spirits and most other fruit spirits rest in inert vessels. Many of the best oak-aged brandies start in new barrels for a year or two, then move to older ones, so the wood frames the fruit without hiding it.

Now to Cognac. It comes from a delimited area just north of Bordeaux, in south-west France. Several grape varieties are allowed, but one dominates: Ugni Blanc. On its own it makes thin, unremarkable wine, yet once distilled it gives a signature aroma of raisins and violets. Its character also changes with where it grows. The Cognac area is divided into six sub-regions, and the finest surround the town of Cognac itself. Grande Champagne is widely considered the best, followed by Petite Champagne and Borderies.

Cognac's distillation is tightly regulated. The grapes are picked in autumn, and all the wine must be distilled by the end of March the following year. Cognac must be double distilled in copper pot stills, and those stills have two rare features. First, they must be heated by a direct flame, today usually gas burners. Second, instead of a modern condenser, they must use a worm tub: a tank of cold water as big as the still itself, with a single coiled copper pipe inside. The parts even have local names: the olive-shaped still head is the chapiteau, and the curving swan neck is the col de cygne.

After distillation, every Cognac must spend at least two years in oak. Almost all are blends of grape varieties, sub-regions and ages, and producers even keep warehouses in different places to create more variety. The oldest spirits, sometimes decades old, are moved into glass demijohns once oak and oxygen have nothing more to give, and then used sparingly to add depth to the most prestigious blends. And a detail that surprises many: most Cognacs are lightly sweetened before bottling, a long-standing local practice.

A Cognac label speaks of age and place. The age terms are VS, VSOP, XO, Napoléon and Hors d'âge, and they always refer to the youngest spirit in the blend: at least two years in oak for VS, four for VSOP, and longer still for the others. In the glass, a VS shows fruit and oak and can feel a little sharp; a VSOP is richer, with first notes of maturity; a fine XO weaves together raisin, flowers, oak and rancio with a silky texture. A sub-region name means all the grapes come from there, and Fine Champagne blends Grande and Petite Champagne, with at least half Grande.

Now Armagnac, France's other great grape brandy, made south of Bordeaux. Here small producers, rather than large companies, are the norm, and the word Château on a label signals a single small estate. Ugni Blanc is again the most planted grape, but local distillers make much more use of other permitted varieties. Baco often gives a characteristic aroma of prunes, while Folle Blanche brings pronounced floral and fruity notes.

The big technical difference is the still. Pot stills are allowed but rare. Most Armagnac comes from a continuous column of its own design, which must be short, with relatively few plates. The spirit therefore leaves the still at a fairly low strength, full of congeners and character. Proof, once again, that a column does not automatically mean a light spirit. Maturation, blending and preparation for bottling are then similar to Cognac, with similar age terms, though the minimum ages differ slightly.

Two styles set Armagnac apart. Vintage Armagnac is made only from grapes of a single harvest, so it is not a blend of different ages; vintages are common here but rare in Cognac. And Blanche is Armagnac that never sees oak: made exactly like the others but bottled clear, a style with no equivalent in Cognac, and one that suits the expressive fruit of Folle Blanche perfectly. On labels, look also for the two key sub-regions, Bas Armagnac and Ténarèze.

Here is a memory tip. Cognac is the symphony orchestra: big houses, strict rules, double pot distillation, a direct flame, a worm tub and a blend of many voices. Armagnac is the folk band: small family estates, a short column, single vintages and even an unaged Blanche. Same grape on the music stand, very different performance.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, fruit must be processed quickly near where it grows; distillers prefer acidic, neutral white grapes, and white pomace is fermented with water while black pomace already contains alcohol. Second, Cognac is mostly Ugni Blanc from north of Bordeaux, double distilled in direct-fired pot stills with a worm tub, aged at least two years in oak, with age terms referring to the youngest spirit. Third, Armagnac, south of Bordeaux, adds Baco and Folle Blanche, is usually made in a short column, and is known for vintages, unaged Blanche, and Bas Armagnac and Ténarèze.

In the last lesson we met France's two great grape brandies. Now we widen the picture with three more fruit spirits, each with a strong identity. First Calvados, the apple brandy of Normandy. Then grappa, Italy's benchmark pomace spirit. And finally pisco, the aromatic grape brandy of Chile and Peru. For each one, ask yourself three questions as we go: what fruit, what still, and what vessel afterwards? Those three answers will carry you through most exam questions on this chapter.

Let's start in the far north of France, in Normandy. The climate there is too cool for grapes to ripen well, so orchards take the place of vineyards. Calvados must be made in specific parts of the region, and it is made from apples and pears. Apples are by far the more important, with pears in a supporting role. Like Tequila, Calvados ties its raw material to a defined area, so every bottle carries a sense of that landscape.

The production follows the classic fruit route. The fruit is pressed, the juice is fermented, and the result is distilled. Producers use a variety of pot stills and short column stills. Both are chosen to give characterful spirits, not light ones; once again, a short column keeps plenty of aroma. Then, like most grape and apple brandies, Calvados is matured in oak. And here comes its personal twist: the oak vessels are usually large.

Why does the size of the vessel matter? Think about the surface of the wood. In a large vessel, each litre of spirit touches much less wood than in a standard barrel, so the oak gives far less flavour. That is why even a very old Calvados still smells clearly and recognisably of apples, with the wood playing a supporting role. Imagine tasting two aged brandies side by side: the one where fresh or baked apple shines through after many years is very likely to be Calvados.

Now we cross the Alps to Italy. Pomace spirits are made all over the world, but Italy has set the benchmark with grappa. The name is protected: only a pomace spirit made in Italy may be called grappa. A spirit made in exactly the same way in France or Spain must use another name. On the label, the word grappa always stands out, sometimes with the name of a grape variety beside it, because many grappas are made from a single variety, while others come from a mix.

Remember from the last lesson how pomace is handled. White grape skins arrive moist with juice and are fermented with water; black grape skins arrive already soaked in alcohol from red winemaking and can be distilled straight away. Either way, the skins give the spirit its signature: pronounced herbaceous notes. Classic grappa is unaged. It rests briefly in inert vessels and is bottled colourless, and young examples can feel a little sharp on the palate. Think of a freshly cut green stem: lively and direct rather than round and mellow.

The best producers move beyond this basic template in two ways. First, they let the grape variety speak. This is easiest to taste in grappa made from aromatic varieties such as Moscato, also known as Muscat, which adds pronounced floral and fruity aromas on top of the herbaceous base. Second, they rest the spirit for a year or more in inert vessels, such as stainless steel or glass. It stays completely colourless, because nothing comes from the vessel, but the texture becomes fuller and smoother. Colourless does not have to mean young.

Now let's fly to South America. Pisco is the grape brandy of Chile and Peru, and it turns the usual brandy logic on its head. Most brandy makers pick acidic, neutral grapes; pisco producers deliberately choose highly aromatic varieties, especially members of the Muscat family. The aim is a spirit that smells vividly of the grape itself. A good pisco brings flowers and ripe fruit to mind before you even take a sip.

To protect those aromas, pisco is distilled in pot stills. Most pisco is unaged, and in Peru this is a legal requirement, so Peruvian pisco never sees wood. The best examples are prized for pure, pronounced fruity and floral aromas. Chile also makes some wood-matured versions, but the time in wood is normally short, so the spirit keeps its vibrant fruit. If the exam asks which country requires pisco to be unaged, the answer is Peru.

Pisco also has a famous role behind the bar. It is the base of the Pisco Sour, a classic of the sour family made with lime juice, sugar syrup and egg white. The egg white gives a smooth, silky texture and a soft foam on top, and the aromatic grape shines through the citrus. It is a lovely example of how the character of a spirit carries into a cocktail.

Before we finish, a quick tour of the rest of the world. Fresh, unaged grape and pomace brandies are made in many countries, with notable examples in Spain, South Africa and Mexico. And Central Europe is famous for pure, expressive spirits made from plums, cherries and berries, usually rested in inert vessels to keep the fruit bright. Some of these fruits give so little juice that, instead of being fermented, they are steeped in neutral spirit and redistilled.

Here is a memory tip: three fruits, three wardrobes. Calvados wears a big oak coat that is loose enough to let the apple breathe. Grappa wears the green of the grape skins, sometimes with a Moscato flower in its buttonhole. Pisco wears nothing but its own perfume, especially in Peru, where wood is not allowed.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Calvados comes from Normandy, mainly from apples with some pears, is made in pot stills or short columns, and is matured in large oak vessels, so the apple stays clear even when old. Second, grappa is a pomace spirit that can only be made in Italy, usually unaged, herbaceous and sometimes sharp; the best show their grape, such as Moscato, or rest a year or more in inert vessels for a smoother texture. Third, pisco comes from Chile and Peru, from aromatic Muscat-family grapes distilled in pot stills, mostly unaged and legally so in Peru, with pure, pronounced fruity and floral aromas.

In this lesson we cross the Atlantic to meet American whiskey. We start with the challenge every whisky maker faces: grain has no sugar, only starch. Then we look at the three American styles with the strongest reputation, Bourbon, Tennessee Whiskey and rye whiskey, and finish by learning to read the words on an American whiskey label. A quick note on spelling: in the United States and Ireland it is usually whiskey with an e, while Scotland and Canada write whisky.

Every whisky in the world shares two traits: it is made from grain, and it is matured in oak. The main grains are barley, corn, wheat and rye. A grain is a seed, and inside it is a store of starch meant to feed the young plant as it sprouts. Yeast cannot ferment starch, so before fermentation the distiller must turn it into sugar. There are two techniques: malting and cooking. Barley is usually malted, while the other grains are cooked and then mixed with malted barley.

With barley, the plant does the work. Kept warm and damp, the grains sprout and release enzymes. After a few days the sprouting grain, called green malt, is heated to stop the growth, and the result is malted barley. It is crushed into a coarse flour and mixed with warm water, and its enzymes convert the starch into sugar, giving a sweet liquid called wort. Corn, rye and wheat are instead crushed, mixed with water and cooked at high temperature, which makes the starch soluble. Once the mix has cooled, a little malted barley is added, and its enzymes are strong enough to convert all the starch.

Now to Bourbon. It can be made anywhere in the United States, but the vast majority comes from Kentucky. The key rule concerns grain: at least fifty-one percent must be corn. Corn on its own gives a fairly soft whiskey with sweetcorn aromas, so distillers add what they call flavouring grains. The particular combination each distillery uses is called the mash bill, and it works like a signature.

Each grain in the mash bill has a job. Malted barley is used in small amounts, mainly for its enzymes. Rye brings spicy, rye-bread notes. Wheat gives a softer, smoother character. So two Bourbons can feel quite different: one with plenty of rye comes across as peppery and lively, while one that uses wheat instead tastes rounder and gentler. When you taste Bourbon, try to guess which flavouring grain is speaking.

Most Bourbon is distilled in column stills, sometimes called beer stills in the industry. But the law keeps the new spirit fairly low in strength: no more than eighty percent alcohol by volume, or one hundred and sixty proof. As we learned earlier, a low distillation strength means plenty of congeners. The spirit must then be matured in new, charred oak barrels. Because they are new, they give a great deal of vanilla, coconut and sweet spice, and the hot Kentucky summers speed up the exchange with the wood.

Put these rules together, and you understand the style. A high share of corn, a low distillation strength and new oak give Bourbon pronounced flavours and a warming, sometimes slightly sharp texture. It is a whiskey built for intensity rather than delicacy. And remember that, once malted or cooked, all the grains of the mash bill are mixed together for the starch conversion: the corn, the flavouring grains and the small share of malted barley that does the converting.

Next, Tennessee Whiskey, a close relative. It shares Bourbon's foundations: at least fifty-one percent corn and maturation in new, charred oak. In fact, it is essentially a straight Bourbon with two differences. First, place: it can only be made and matured in the state of Tennessee. Second, an extra step called the Lincoln County Process. Before going into barrel, the new spirit trickles slowly through a deep bed of maple-wood charcoal.

What does that charcoal do? It softens and smooths the young spirit before it ever meets the wood. Think of fine sandpaper rounding off the corners of a freshly cut plank. The typical result is a whiskey with a notably smooth texture and aromas of sweetcorn, vanilla and sometimes banana. The process is required by law for Tennessee Whiskey, with a single distillery exempted. And don't confuse it with the activated charcoal used for vodka: here the whiskey keeps its character, and still gains its colour from the barrel.

Now rye whiskey. It is made in almost exactly the same way as Bourbon, with one decisive change: at least fifty-one percent of the grain must be rye rather than corn. That big share of rye transforms the glass. Where Bourbon speaks of sweetcorn and vanilla, rye leans towards lively spice, lemon zest and rye bread, often with a drier, more peppery finish. Rye is enjoying a strong revival: more and more distillers are making it, and the style is evolving quickly.

Finally, the label. Straight means the whiskey has been matured for at least two years in new oak barrels, with no added colour or flavouring; the term can be used for rye as well as Bourbon. And if a straight Bourbon contains whiskey younger than four years, an age statement must appear on the label. So a straight Bourbon with no age statement is at least four years old. Proof, as we saw in the first lesson, is double the alcohol by volume: ninety proof means forty-five percent, one hundred proof means fifty.

Sour mash describes a technique: the acidic residue left in the base of the column still is added back to the next fermentation. The law does not require it, but it is very widely used by American distillers. Two more terms suggest higher quality. Single barrel means the whiskey was bottled from one barrel the distiller judged exceptional, so each release can vary a little. Small batch means a blend of a small number of selected casks; but beware, how small a batch must be is not defined by law.

Here is a memory tip: think of fifty-one as the magic number. Fifty-one percent corn makes Bourbon, fifty-one percent rye makes rye whiskey, and Bourbon's rules plus Tennessee plus maple charcoal make Tennessee Whiskey. Then add two more numbers for the label: two years makes a whiskey straight, and under four years a straight Bourbon must show its age.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, grain starch must become sugar: barley by malting, other grains by cooking and adding malted barley for its enzymes. Second, Bourbon needs at least fifty-one percent corn, distillation to no more than eighty percent and new charred oak; Tennessee Whiskey adds the state of Tennessee and maple charcoal filtering; rye needs fifty-one percent rye and tastes of spice, lemon zest and rye bread. Third, on the label, straight means at least two years in new oak with nothing added, proof is double the percentage, sour mash recycles still residue, and small batch has no legal definition.

In this lesson we travel to Scotland, home of some of the most famous whiskies in the world. We start with the one rule every Scotch must follow. Then we look closely at malt whisky, where barley, peat, still shape and casks all shape the flavour. After that we meet grain whisky and Blended Scotch, learn the key words on a Scotch label, and finish with the five whisky regions and what they can, and cannot, tell you.

First, the ground rule. To be called Scotch, a whisky must be made in Scotland and matured in oak barrels for at least three years. This applies to every type, from the rarest single malt to the simplest blend. Scotland's cool climate sets the pace: the spirit moves in and out of the wood more slowly than in Kentucky's hot summers, so colour and oak flavour build up gently. A Scotch therefore needs more time to reach a similar maturity, and three years is only a starting point. Many stay in cask for far longer.

Now, malt whisky. It is made only from malted barley and distilled in pot stills, nearly always twice. A single malt must come from one distillery, but don't imagine it as the contents of one cask: it is usually a complex blend of older and younger spirits, all from the same place. The barley gives every malt whisky a distinct malty, cereal flavour, and sometimes something much more dramatic.

That something is peat smoke. Peat is damp, partly decayed vegetation cut from the ground. Once dried, it can be burnt to give a very aromatic smoke. If peat is used as the fuel to heat the green malt at the end of malting, its smoke clings to the grains, and that smokiness carries right through into the whisky. So a smoky whisky is born in the malting, long before the still.

The still itself does not create flavour, but its shape and height influence the style. Particularly short stills tend to give spirits with more pronounced aromas, while notably tall stills give a lighter style. Picture the vapour climbing: in a tall still, the heavier compounds struggle to reach the top and fall back, so only the lighter ones make it over to the condenser.

Then comes oak, the other great source of flavour. New oak is rarely used in Scotland; second-hand casks are preferred. Most come from the Bourbon industry, and they give subtle coconut, vanilla and spice. A smaller number are ex-Sherry casks from Jerez in southern Spain, seasoned there with wine before being shipped to Scotland, and they are linked with dried fruit and orange peel. See how the two countries connect: Bourbon law demands new oak, so each barrel serves Bourbon only once, and Scotland happily gives it a second life.

Some malts also receive a wood finish. Near the end of maturation, the whisky is moved into a different cask for a relatively short time. That finishing cask previously held a wine or a spirit, such as Port or Sherry, and the liquid still soaked in its staves seeps out, adding flavour and sometimes colour. On the label you might read something like Sherry cask finish.

Now grain whisky. It is made from a mix of grains, distilled to a high strength in column stills, and it has a light flavour intensity. It is very rarely sold on its own. Almost all of it goes into Blended Scotch Whisky, which is a blend of malt whisky and grain whisky from different distilleries. Think of grain whisky as the canvas, and the malts as the bright colours painted on it.

The blender's aims are the ones we met earlier in the course: consistency from batch to batch, and complexity that no single component has on its own. That needs a wide palette: bold and delicate malts, peated and unpeated, young and mature, from different casks. Most Blended Scotch is young, little more than three years old, and made for everyday drinking. Yet some outstanding blends, built on very old components, rank among the finest whiskies Scotland makes. Blend describes a method, not a quality level.

Time to read a label. Single means the whisky comes from one distillery. Malt means made only from malted barley and distilled in pot stills. So Single Malt Scotch Whisky is malt from one distillery, while Blended Scotch Whisky signals a mix of malt and grain. An age statement, say twelve years, always refers to the youngest whisky in the bottle: everything inside is at least that old.

Three more terms describe what has not been done. A whisky can turn hazy when cold or when water is added, so many producers chill-filter it before bottling. Non-chill-filtered means this step was skipped, because some believe it also strips out flavour and texture. Natural colour means no caramel was used: all the colour came from the casks. And cask strength means the whisky was bottled without dilution, often well above forty percent, for enthusiasts who like to add their own few drops of water.

Finally, the regions. Scotland has five whisky regions: Highland, Speyside, Lowland, Campbeltown and the island of Islay. They often appear on single malt labels but rarely on blends. Here is the catch: the only thing a region name tells you with certainty is where the distillery is. It is not a reliable guide to style, because each distillery's choices of malt, stills and casks matter more. The exception is Islay, off the west coast, where the vast majority of whiskies have the distinct smoky aroma of peat.

Here is a memory tip. Picture a Scotch as a three-layer cake. The bottom layer is the barley, malty and sometimes smoky. The middle layer is the still, short for richness, tall for lightness. The icing is the cask: vanilla from ex-Bourbon, dried fruit from ex-Sherry, with an extra sprinkle if there is a finish. And if the cake smells of a bonfire, think Islay.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, every Scotch is made in Scotland and aged at least three years in oak; single malt is malted barley, pot-distilled, from one distillery, with flavour from peat, still shape and casks, mostly ex-Bourbon, some ex-Sherry, sometimes with a wood finish. Second, grain whisky is column-distilled to high strength and light in flavour, and Blended Scotch combines malt and grain from different distilleries. Third, on the label, the age statement is the youngest whisky, non-chill-filtered, natural colour and cask strength mean less intervention, and of the five regions only Islay reliably signals peat smoke.

Welcome back. So far we have travelled through American whiskey and Scotch whisky. In this lesson we complete the world tour with three more whisky nations: Canada, Ireland and Japan. Each one borrows ideas from its neighbours, yet each has found its own voice. We will look at how Canadian blends are built, why Irish whiskey is often so gentle, and how Japan took the Scottish model and gave it a purer accent. Keep the American and Scottish lessons in mind: we will lean on them constantly.

Let us begin in Canada. A first detail about spelling: Canadian whisky is written without an e, just like in Scotland, while Americans and the Irish usually write whiskey with an e. Spelling aside, the key fact about Canada is that its production is dominated by blends. A Canadian distiller rarely bottles one single type of spirit. Instead, it builds a brand by mixing different whiskies, each made separately for a particular role in the final recipe.

How is a typical Canadian blend put together? Picture a soup. The largest part is a light stock: a whisky usually made from corn and distilled to a high strength, so it carries only a light flavour. Into that stock goes a small amount of something much tastier: a pronounced whisky, distilled to a lower strength, which the trade calls a flavouring whisky. The light corn whisky gives volume and softness; the flavouring whisky gives personality. The art lies in the proportions.

The most common flavouring whisky in Canada is made from rye. And here comes a classic exam trap. In Canada, a blend may be labelled Canadian Rye Whisky, or simply Rye Whisky, whatever the amount of rye in the final blend. Compare that with the United States, where a rye whiskey must be made from at least fifty-one percent rye. So the same word, rye, promises a lot on an American label, and much less on a Canadian one.

Canadian styles cover a wide range. The big international brands, with a high share of corn whisky, tend to be very soft and easy, with little to challenge the drinker. Whiskies that contain a higher share of spirit made from other grains are more pronounced and full of flavour. A practical tip for the bar: if a guest finds a Canadian whisky too gentle, look for a style richer in flavouring whiskies, rather than abandoning the country altogether.

Now we cross the Atlantic to Ireland. Most Irish whiskeys are blends too, but of a different kind: they combine spirit from pot stills with spirit from column stills. Ireland also makes some malt whiskey in pot stills. Overall, the Irish style is lighter than the Scottish one. One reason is that peat, so important on an island like Islay, is rarely used in Ireland, even for malt whiskey. So smoky aromas are the exception rather than the rule.

The second reason for this lightness is triple distillation. In Scotland, malt whisky usually passes through a pot still twice. The Irish tradition is to distil malt whiskey three times in pot stills. Each extra pass raises the strength a little and removes more of the heavier congeners, so the spirit becomes cleaner and more delicate. Think of a fabric that feels softer every time it goes through another wash: it loses a little body, but gains smoothness.

A third Irish hallmark is the use of unmalted barley alongside malted barley. You will remember that barley normally has to be malted so its enzymes can turn starch into sugar. In Ireland, some of the barley is used raw, and the malted barley in the mash supplies enough enzymes for all of it. This unmalted grain gives aromas often described as spicy, fruity or oily, and a distinctive texture on the palate. And remember that Ireland is changing fast: the number of distilleries has grown strongly in recent years, and so has the range of styles.

Our last stop is Japan. Here the reference point is Scotland. Japanese distillers make grain whisky in column stills and malt whisky in pot stills, exactly as the Scots do. With these two base spirits, they produce and sell both malt whiskies and blended whiskies. So if you already understand the difference between a malt and a blend in Scotland, you already understand the main Japanese categories.

Similar, however, does not mean identical. Japanese whiskies have a character of their own. They tend towards a purer, cleaner style, and they usually show less of the malty, cereal flavour that is common in many Scotch whiskies. Imagine two breads made from the same flour: one a rustic country loaf, the other a very fine white loaf. The ingredients are close, but the result feels more polished. That is a good picture of Japanese whisky beside its Scottish model.

Here is a memory tip to tie the five whisky nations together. The United States is about corn, rye and new charred oak. Scotland is about malt, grain and used casks. Canada is the soup: a light corn base seasoned with flavouring whiskies. Ireland is the extra wash: triple distillation and little peat. And Japan is the fine white loaf: the Scottish recipe, made purer. If you can say those five sentences, most exam questions on whisky origins become easy.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Canadian whisky is mostly blended from a light, high-strength corn whisky and a small share of flavouring whisky, often rye, and it can be called rye whatever the rye content. Second, Irish whiskey is mostly a blend of pot and column still spirits; it is usually lighter than Scotch, rarely peated, and its malts are traditionally triple distilled, with unmalted barley adding spicy, fruity, oily notes. Third, Japan follows the Scottish model of malt and grain whiskies, but in a purer style with fewer malty, cereal notes.

In this lesson we sail to the Caribbean and beyond: the subject is rum, which ranges from colourless, unaged, light spirits to deep brown ones marked by long years in wood. We will cover five things: the raw material, stills and the idea of light and heavy marks, the three colour styles, the great historical traditions, and the words on a rum label. It is a big chapter, so let us take it one step at a time.

First, the raw material. Every rum is made from sugar cane, a tall plant that grows wherever it is hot enough and lives for several years. Its thick stems are cut close to the ground, so the roots stay and new stems can grow. Those stems are full of sugar that is easy to extract: crush them in a mill and out comes a sweet liquid, sugar cane juice. Some distillers ferment this juice straight away. Rums made this way have pronounced vegetal, grassy and fruity aromas, like the smell of a freshly cut stalk.

Most rum, however, is made from molasses. When the sugar industry boils cane juice, sugar crystals form and are collected. What remains is a thick, sticky residue: molasses. Its quality varies. Molasses taken early in the refining process is richer and better than the exhausted residue left at the end. Because it is so concentrated in sugar, molasses must be diluted with water before yeast can work. Fermentation then creates alcohol and congeners, and many producers try to encourage fruity esters. Jamaica goes furthest: very aromatic fermentations followed by pot still distillation give high-ester rums with an intense, almost pungent fruitiness.

Second, distillation. Rum has remarkably few production rules. The main limit is that it must not be distilled so far that it becomes a neutral spirit. Pot stills and columns of every design are used, sometimes side by side in the same distillery. To make sense of this variety, the trade uses a simple idea. Each individual newly made rum is called a mark. Marks fall into two families: light marks and heavy marks.

Light marks come from column stills at high strength, often above ninety percent alcohol by volume, so they have a light aroma intensity. They form the base of many unaged rums, and after time in oak they are also important in golden rums. Heavy marks are distilled to a lower strength, usually in pot stills, many of them unique designs. They can be very fruity, or rich and savoury. Some heavy marks come from short columns, as with many cane juice rums, to keep the cane character. Almost every rum is a blend of marks, even when it comes from one distillery, and the style depends on which family dominates.

After distillation, a rum can stay unaged or go into oak, more often reused casks than new ones. The finest heavy marks, after long ageing, develop bruised fruit, over-ripe banana and rancio notes, a savoury, leathery richness. Many are too intense to bottle alone, so blenders use them for depth. Then come three possible finishing touches. A briefly aged rum may be filtered through activated charcoal to remove its colour while keeping some smoothness. Caramel may be added for colour. And many rums, especially oak-aged ones, are sweetened. Sugar flatters fruit and rancio, but too much smothers the rum.

Third, the colour styles. Because the laws say so little, rums are often sorted by colour. It is a handy, visual guide, but remember that colour can be taken out by filtration or added with caramel. White rums are colourless, even if some have been aged and then filtered; most are light, a few very aromatic. Golden or amber rums take most of their colour from oak, with a touch of caramel for consistency, and often have medium sweetness. Their makers' key decision is the ratio of light to heavy marks.

Dark rums are two very different worlds. A minority are golden rums aged for a long time, which turn brown and develop black banana, leather and meaty rancio flavours. The majority owe their colour mainly to large doses of caramel and are young or even unaged. The palate gives them away: the best show plenty of cane character, but none of the aromas or texture of long ageing. So when you taste a dark rum, ask yourself: is this the colour of time, or the colour of caramel?

Fourth, the traditions. The Caribbean was colonised by Britain, France and Spain, and each left a rum style. The British style grew from the Navy's daily ration of rum with water, sugar and lime, which needed a characterful rum built on heavy marks. Jamaica supplies very fruity, high-ester marks; Guyana rich, deep marks for long ageing; Barbados a smoother style. The French style belongs to Martinique and Guadeloupe. France favoured beet sugar, so the islands' cane juice was distilled instead, in short columns. The whites are among the most pronounced rums made; the golden ones are usually dry or off-dry.

The Spanish style aims for light to medium intensity and a smooth palate. Its white rums are described as Cuban style, the most popular white rum style today. In Cuba, producers used the new column stills to make high-strength marks, then gave them a short spell in oak for a softer mouthfeel, perfect for cocktails. Spanish-style golden rums use mostly light marks, show clear oak vanilla and often a little sugar. Panama, Guatemala and Venezuela follow this style. Finally, Brazil is the world's largest rum producer, thanks to cachaça, a cane juice rum, mostly unaged, lightly sweetened and drunk at home.

Fifth, the label. Rum terms are loosely defined, with no single set of rules for every country. Age statements are the clearest case: a number may refer to the youngest rum, the oldest, or some kind of average, depending on the producer. Two terms, however, reliably signal cane juice: rhum agricole, used in the Caribbean only for Martinique and Guadeloupe, and cachaça, from Brazil. Finally, overproof means an unusually high strength. British sailors tested rum with gunpowder: it only burned from about fifty-seven percent alcohol by volume, defined as one hundred proof. The word survives on labels, but it is no longer an official measure, and differs from the American proof system.

Here is a memory tip: think of rum as a blender's spice rack. Light marks are the salt, there in quantity to give body without shouting. Heavy marks are the spices, used sparingly for character. Caramel, charcoal and sugar are the presentation. Look at any rum and ask how much salt, how much spice, and how it was dressed.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, all rum comes from sugar cane, mostly via molasses; cane juice rums such as rhum agricole and cachaça smell vegetal and grassy. Second, rum is almost always a blend of light and heavy marks, and may be filtered, coloured or sweetened, so colour alone tells you little. Third, the British style is heavy and characterful, the French style uses cane juice, the Spanish style is light and smooth; and rum age statements are not strictly regulated.

In this lesson we travel to Mexico, the home of agave spirits. At their heart all of them share the earthy, powerful aromas of the agave plant, yet producers create very different styles from it. We will follow the agave from the field to the still, then look closely at the two great geographical indications: Tequila, with its single variety and its ageing categories, and Mezcal, with its many agaves, its smoke and its three traditional classes.

Let us start with the plant. Agave is native to Central America and there are hundreds of species. All share the same shape: a hard core from which long, spiky, waxy leaves grow. In that core the plant stores its energy as inulin, a kind of carbohydrate. Agave lives a long time, often many years, and then flowers just once, using up all its reserves before it dies. So the grower's skill is timing: the plant is harvested just before it flowers.

Why then? Because at that moment the agave has the most inulin, and also its most complex aromas, which recall bell pepper, vegetables and black pepper. At harvest the plant is cut from its roots and the leaves are trimmed away. What remains is the core, called the piña, because it looks like a giant pineapple. Now comes the key technical point. Inulin cannot be fermented as it is. Just as grain starch has to be converted, inulin must be turned into sugar, and here the tool is heat. That is why the piña is always cooked.

There are two traditional cooking methods. For Tequila, the piñas are steamed slowly in brick ovens. For Mezcal, they are often roasted in stone-lined pits. Many Tequila producers now use pressurised steam ovens called autoclaves, which are much faster but can scorch the agave. After cooking, the piñas are crushed, traditionally with a huge stone wheel and today often with mechanical mills, and rinsed with water to wash out every last bit of sugar. Making up this sweet liquid ready for fermentation is called formulation.

Now fermentation and distillation. The best producers add some of the piña fibres to the fermenting liquid, to push the agave character further. Agave spirits can be made in pot or column stills, but quality Tequila and Mezcal are usually double distilled in pot stills: large modern ones for Tequila, small and often home-made ones for Mezcal. Some are collected at very low strengths, below sixty percent alcohol by volume, which keeps plenty of flavour. Afterwards, most agave spirits rest in inert vessels or very large oak vats. Small barrels are rare, because agave aromas, however powerful, are easily drowned by oak.

Let us move to the label. In Mexico, people loosely call every agave spirit mezcal. But there are also legally defined geographical indications, rather like Cognac and Armagnac, which say where the agave may grow and how the spirit must be made. The two most important are Tequila and, confusingly, Mezcal. On a label, the word Mezcal refers only to that specific indication. The two are very different: Tequila is dominated by large companies, while Mezcal is still mainly made by small producers.

Tequila is the biggest agave spirit by volume, yet it may use only one variety: blue agave, which takes seven to ten years to mature. It must be grown in one of five Mexican states, and the most important is Jalisco, where blue agave comes from. One variety does not mean one flavour, though. Blue agave changes with its surroundings, and agave grown at altitude can be fruitier. The finest Tequilas come from agave slow-cooked in brick ovens, fermented with fibres, double distilled in pot stills and collected at low strength, giving a warming texture and an intense agave character.

The most important word on a Tequila label is one hundred percent agave. It means every fermented sugar came from the agave. A bottle that just says Tequila needs only fifty-one percent agave sugars; the rest can come from other sources, which dilute the agave flavour. These are sometimes called mixto, but that is not a legal label term. Then come the categories. Blanco, or Silver, has no ageing requirement. Gold is unaged, but coloured and softened with abocado, a caramel-based additive designed to mimic the effect of wood. Reposado means at least two months in oak, usually large vats. Añejo means at least one year in oak barrels, and Extra Añejo at least three years.

Now Mezcal. The geographical indication covers several states, but the most important by far is Oaxaca, in the south, where the vast majority is made. Unlike Tequila, Mezcal may be made from several agave species. The most used is espadín, the main variety of Oaxaca. All agaves share earthy, vegetal aromas, but expert tasters can pick out differences between species. Then comes the signature: smoke. A fire is lit in a stone-lined pit, and once it has burnt out the piñas are laid on the hot stones, covered with earth and left to cook. Steaming adds no flavour; roasting adds smoke, of very variable intensity.

Three factors together give the best Mezcal its unique mix of smoky, earthy and vegetal flavours: pit roasting, fibres in the fermentation, and distillation in simple pot stills to a low strength. To help drinkers spot traditional methods, three categories exist. A spirit labelled simply Mezcal may use any cooking method, including steam ovens, and any still, columns included. Artisanal Mezcal allows only pits or brick ovens, limited mills, fermentation with fibres in stone, wood or clay vessels, and directly heated metal or clay pot stills. Ancestral Mezcal goes further: pits only, no mechanical mills, fibres in both fermentation and distillation, and directly heated clay stills.

Here is a memory tip. Think of the piña as a pumpkin. Steam it gently and you get pure, sweet vegetable flavour: that is Tequila. Roast it in the embers and you get the same vegetable, but smoky and earthy: that is Mezcal. And for the ageing ladder of Tequila, count up: no time for Blanco, two months for Reposado, one year for Añejo, three years for Extra Añejo.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, agave stores inulin in its core, the piña, which must be cooked to turn inulin into sugar: steamed for Tequila, roasted in pits for Mezcal. Second, Tequila uses only blue agave from five states, mainly Jalisco; one hundred percent agave means all the sugar is from agave, while plain Tequila needs only fifty-one percent; and the categories run from Blanco and Gold to Reposado, Añejo and Extra Añejo. Third, Mezcal comes mainly from Oaxaca, may use several agaves, especially espadín, is typically smoky, and has three classes: Mezcal, Artisanal and Ancestral.

In this lesson we turn to the most neutral of all the great spirits: vodka. Born in Eastern Europe, it is now one of the best-selling spirits almost everywhere. Its secret is not a strong personality, but the opposite: because it clashes with nothing, it mixes with almost anything, from a simple long drink to a complex cocktail. We will look at the raw materials, at how starch becomes sugar, at the column still and the strengths it must reach, at what happens after distillation, and finally at vodka's two styles and its traditional homelands.

First, the raw materials. In theory vodka can be made from anything of agricultural origin. In practice, cost and what customers expect narrow the list to a few, mainly grains and potatoes. Grains are one of the key crops of Eastern Europe, and distillers use barley, wheat and rye. But none of these grains contains sugar. Their carbohydrate is starch, and yeast cannot ferment starch. So, as with whisky, the starch must first be converted into sugar.

How is that done? The traditional answer is malted barley, which supplies the enzymes that break starch into sugar. Many vodka distillers today take a shortcut: they buy commercially prepared enzymes and add them to grain that has been crushed and cooked in water. Think of a baker who uses ready-made yeast rather than keeping a sourdough starter: the result is reliable and the work is quicker. Once the starch has become sugar, yeast is added and fermentation proceeds as for any other spirit.

Potatoes are the other classic raw material, especially in Poland. The potato is the part of the plant that stores starch underground, so it too needs a two-step conversion. First, the potatoes are cooked in water until they fall apart completely, which makes the starch soluble and gives a cloudy liquid full of dissolved starch. Then bought-in enzymes are added to turn that starch into sugar. Beyond grains and potatoes, some producers experiment with other materials, either to use the cheapest option available or to stand out. Grapes have been a notable example in recent years.

Second, distillation. Vodka is made from neutral spirit, distilled to a very high strength: at least ninety-five percent alcohol by volume in the United States and ninety-six percent in the European Union. At these levels so few congeners survive that the aroma is described as neutral. Only one kind of still can get there: a column still with enough plates. A pot still alone never can. Some distillers add extra distillation steps to make the spirit even purer and smoother, and the whole process normally runs continuously.

There are some interesting variations. A few small distillers, working in batches, make low wines in a pot still and then complete the second distillation in a column. This has no effect on the final flavour, because the column does the decisive work. Other producers do not distil from scratch at all. Neutral spirit is a widely traded commodity, and a producer could simply buy it and dilute it with water. The problem is that vodka made this way can feel slightly rough.
