The solution is clever. The producer dilutes some or all of the bought-in spirit and runs it through what looks like a pot still, but is actually a hybrid still: a pot linked to a rectifying column. In effect, this is one more column distillation, which purifies the spirit further and gives it a smoother, silkier texture. So when you hear that a vodka was distilled in a pot still, remember that the texture, not the aroma, is usually what changes.

Third, what happens after distillation. Vodka is kept in inert vessels: it is not aged in oak. Many producers then simply dilute it, arguing that distillation alone gives the purity and smoothness they want. Others use two extra techniques. The first is filtration through activated charcoal, which removes any remaining unwanted congeners. The second is additives, bought from specialist suppliers and tailored to each brand, used to create the desired texture and sometimes a very faint aroma.

The final step is dilution, and it matters more than you might think. Most vodka is sold at forty percent alcohol by volume, so nearly sixty percent of each bottle is water added after distillation. With a spirit this delicate, there is nowhere to hide: even tiny impurities in the water could spoil the neutral aromas and the smooth texture. That is why vodka producers take water quality so seriously, more than in almost any other spirit.

Fourth, the styles. Unflavoured vodka comes in two broad styles. Neutral vodkas have the lightest possible flavour. They are not completely tasteless, but they should be smooth, light and dry. Characterful vodkas keep a little more flavour and often a fuller, more mouth-filling texture. Even so, their aromas remain so delicate that they can still be described as neutral; the difference lies mostly in how the vodka feels in the mouth. By combining delicate flavours with a smooth, full texture, producers create many subtly different premium vodkas.

Two last points. Here is a useful tasting clue: if an unflavoured vodka shows aromas that honestly cannot be called neutral, they were almost certainly added after distillation. Flavoured vodkas are a separate family, which we will meet with flavoured spirits. And on origin, vodka is historically linked to Russia, Poland, Finland and Sweden. They still make large volumes, and many highly regarded vodkas come from there. But today vodka is made all over the world at every level of quality, and almost every producing country has outstanding examples.

Here is a memory tip. Think of vodka as a white shirt. All white shirts look the same from across the room; the difference is in the fabric when you touch it. A neutral vodka is crisp cotton, a characterful one is soft brushed cotton. And just as a white shirt shows every stain, vodka shows every flaw, which is why the column, the filtration and the water all have to be perfect.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, vodka can come from any agricultural material, but mainly grains such as barley, wheat and rye, or potatoes in Poland; their starch is converted to sugar with malted barley or, more often, bought-in enzymes. Second, vodka is a neutral spirit distilled to at least ninety-five percent in the United States or ninety-six percent in the European Union, which requires a column still; it may be charcoal filtered, given additives, and is diluted with very pure water. Third, the two styles are neutral and characterful, the difference being mostly texture, and the traditional homelands are Russia, Poland, Finland and Sweden.

Welcome to the first lesson on flavoured spirits, and we begin with the most famous of them: gin. With gin the logic of spirit making changes. Until now, flavour came mostly from the raw material, the fermentation, the still and the oak. With gin, the flavour is added to a spirit that already exists. In this lesson we look at the botanicals, at the base spirit and how the rules differ between Europe and the United States, at the three ways of redistilling with botanicals, and at the label terms London Dry, Distilled Gin and Old Tom.

First, the botanicals. This word covers the plant ingredients used to flavour gin: herbs, seeds, roots, peels and spices. Of all of them, only one is required by law: juniper. Its berries give gin that resinous, pine-like scent that makes it recognisable straight away. Everything else is the distiller's choice, and there is no limit on what can be used. In practice, though, a few botanicals appear in almost every recipe, and you should know them by name.

The four classic companions of juniper are coriander seed, citrus peel, angelica root and orris root. Coriander seed brings spicy, slightly citrusy notes. Citrus peel, such as lemon or orange, adds freshness and lift. Angelica and orris, both roots, bring earthy, floral tones, and they help to bind the other aromas together, rather like the foundations that hold a house in place. In recent years, distillers have used the freedom of the rules to create a huge variety of styles: floral, spicy, citrus-led, or built around local herbs and unusual fruits.

Gin can also be made by simply adding artificial flavourings to a spirit, but the best gins are made by redistillation with real botanicals. After flavouring, most gins rest in inert vessels, are diluted and bottled colourless. There is, however, a small but growing trend to age gin in oak. These gins have a pale lemon colour and some flavour from the wood on top of the botanicals. So if you see a golden gin on a back bar, it is worth asking whether it has spent time in a cask.

Second, the base spirit. Gin does not start from a raw material in the field, but from a finished spirit. Almost all gin distillers start with neutral spirit, highly rectified and with no real character of its own. The reason is simple: on a neutral background, like a blank white canvas, the colours of juniper and the other botanicals stand out clearly. If the base spirit already had a strong taste, it would compete with the botanicals.

In the European Union, this choice is not just a habit, it is the law: gin must be made from neutral spirit. In the United States the rules are more relaxed. There, distillers may also use other distilled spirits with some character, or even distil gin directly from a fermented alcoholic liquid, without making a neutral spirit first. This difference may sound technical, but it has a direct effect on how label terms are used on each side of the Atlantic, as we will see in a moment.

Third, the three approaches to redistillation. In the first, the most direct, the neutral spirit is diluted with water and put into a pot still together with the botanicals, which sit in the liquid. Some distillers leave the botanicals to steep in the spirit for a while before heating begins. The longer the contact with the alcohol, the more flavour is extracted, and the fuller and more intense the gin becomes. It is like brewing a herbal tea: leave the bag in a few extra minutes and the cup becomes much stronger.

In the second approach, the botanicals are placed in a basket fitted in the pipe that connects the still to the condenser. They never touch the boiling liquid. Only the alcoholic vapour passes through them, picking up their aromas on the way. Because there is no contact with hot liquid, less flavour is extracted and the gin is lighter and more delicate. Stills built this way are sometimes called Carterhead stills, a name worth recognising in an exam question.

The third approach is to distil some or all botanicals separately. When botanicals are distilled together, they interact, and their flavours change and evolve during the distillation. Distilled alone, each one gives a purer flavour. Some distillers run most of their botanicals together and then add one separate distillate so that a particular note stands out. Others go all the way, distilling every botanical individually and blending them at the end, like a perfumer assembling a fragrance from separate essences.

Fourth, the label terms. London Dry Gin, or simply Dry Gin, is the most tightly defined style in the European Union. All its flavour must come from redistillation: nothing can be added afterwards, and no sugar may be added. Despite its name, it is not a place of origin. A London Dry can be made anywhere, as long as it follows the method. Distilled Gin is trickier: its meaning changes across the Atlantic. In the European Union it is a gin redistilled with botanicals that may then receive further flavourings. In the United States, Distilled Gin means that all the flavour must come from redistillation, which is closer to the European London Dry.

Finally, Old Tom. This style is older than dry gin and dates from before tastes moved towards dryness. It is not legally defined, but on a label it normally signals that the gin has been sweetened. That matters at the bar: if a historic cocktail recipe calls for Old Tom and you use a London Dry instead, the drink will be drier and sharper than intended.

Here is a memory tip for the three redistillation methods: think of making tea. Botanicals in the liquid, especially after steeping, are the tea bag left in the cup: full and strong. Botanicals in a basket in the vapour are the steam from the kettle passing through the leaves: light and delicate. Separate distillation is a tea blender who brews each leaf on its own and mixes the cups at the end: pure and precise.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, juniper is the only compulsory botanical, usually joined by coriander, citrus peel, angelica and orris, and the best gins are made by redistillation. Second, in the European Union gin must start from neutral spirit, while in the United States other spirits or direct distillation are allowed. Third, London Dry gets all its flavour from redistillation and is never sweetened, wherever it is made; Distilled Gin may have flavours added afterwards in the European Union but not in the United States; and Old Tom usually means a sweetened gin.

In this lesson we explore the wider world of flavoured spirits beyond gin. We will start with the techniques that every producer can choose from: natural or artificial flavours, and natural or artificial colours. Then we will visit four families: spiced rum, flavoured vodka, the aniseed spirits of the Mediterranean, with pastis and absinthe, and finally bitters, which come as aperitifs, digestifs and cocktail bitters. Along the way, notice how the same few techniques explain an enormous range of bottles.

First, flavour. Added flavours fall into two families: natural and artificial. Natural flavours come from fruit or from botanicals, the broad term for the herbs and spices used by distillers. Producers can extract these flavours themselves, or buy ready-made natural flavourings from specialist suppliers and blend them into their spirit. When they do the work themselves, two techniques dominate: maceration and redistillation.

Maceration means soaking the fruit or botanical in alcohol, for anything from a few hours to several months, sometimes with gentle heat to extract more. If a very strong spirit is used, it is usually diluted first, because alcohol that is too strong can pull out unpleasant flavours. Maceration extracts colour and a broad range of flavours, but it cannot isolate one particular aroma. A spirit flavoured this way is sometimes called a tincture.

Redistillation puts a diluted neutral spirit back into a pot still with the fruit or botanicals, sometimes after a short maceration. As the liquid heats, the most volatile aromas come off first and the least volatile last, so the distiller chooses the hearts cut at the moment the wanted aromas appear. The result is called a distillate. Some botanicals are damaged by the heat of a normal still, so producers use a vacuum still: under vacuum, liquids boil at lower temperatures, and fragile flavours such as cucumber are captured much better.

Artificial flavours are man-made, but they imitate flavours found in nature. They are bought from specialist suppliers and simply blended into the base spirit, a technique known as cold compounding. Colour follows the same logic. Natural colour from plants is extracted by maceration, but it is unstable and can vary from bottle to bottle, which most customers would not accept. So even premium producers often use some approved artificial colouring, which explains the vivid shades seen in many liqueurs.

Now our families. Spiced rum is a very popular style. The base is usually a golden rum that has been sweetened, with spices added. Few producers reveal their recipes, but vanilla and cinnamon are among the flavours openly declared by several brands. If natural flavours are used, maceration is the likely technique: redistilling would strip the colour and damage the character of a genuinely aged rum.

Flavoured vodka has two sides. The traditional side belongs to Eastern Europe, where vodka has been flavoured for centuries with honey, fruit and spices, almost always by maceration. Some of these old recipes survive; the best known is vodka flavoured with bison grass, an aromatic herb. The modern side is a recent boom: nearly every vodka brand now has at least one flavoured version, with vanilla, fruit, pepper or even chilli. Inexpensive brands usually rely on artificial or ready-made natural flavourings. Premium producers work with the real ingredients: they macerate fruit or botanicals in neutral spirit and then redistil, giving pure, precise flavours.

Next, the aniseed spirits, made all around the Mediterranean: pastis and absinthe in France, ouzo in Greece, raki in Turkey. They share a compound called anethole, which gives the typical aniseed taste. It comes mainly from three plants: aniseed, fennel and star anise. These spirits usually start from neutral spirit, are unaged, and are coloured with both natural and artificial colours. Anethole also has a visible effect. When water is added, it comes out of solution and forms a milky, opaque suspension. This clouding is called louching, and because these drinks are served heavily diluted, watching the louche appear is part of the ritual.

Pastis is the best known of them. As well as aniseed, fennel and star anise, it must contain liquorice. It must also be sweetened, so most pastis is medium or sweet, and it is usually coloured yellow, green or green-brown. Picture it served the traditional way: a small measure in a tall glass, topped with plenty of cold water, turning from clear gold to a soft, cloudy yellow.

Pastis rose to fame when absinthe was banned. Absinthe was outlawed for decades after social and political pressure in the late nineteenth century. It is allowed again, but has no legal definition, so nothing is guaranteed. The traditional method is close to pastis, with two differences: absinthe is not sweetened, because drinkers sweeten it to taste, and it should contain wormwood, a plant with a floral aroma and a bitter taste. It is bottled very strong, but meant to be diluted to no more than the strength of wine.

Finally, bitters. These are spirits, usually with a neutral base, that have an obvious bitter taste from one or more botanicals, such as quinine, gentian, bitter orange or artichoke. Here is a useful tasting fact: bitterness cannot be smelled, only detected by the tongue. Other aromatic botanicals and sugar are added to balance it.

There are three broad categories. Aperitif bitters are often brightly coloured, with bitterness balanced by sweetness, and are drunk before a meal, usually in a long drink or a cocktail. Digestif bitters have pronounced bitterness and intense flavour; they began as digestive aids and are still enjoyed after meals. Cocktail bitters are high in strength, very concentrated and intensely bitter, and are used only in dashes to add an extra dimension to a drink.

Here is a memory tip for bitters: think of a meal. Before dinner, a bright, bittersweet glass with soda opens the appetite: aperitif. After dinner, a dark, intense sip helps you recover: digestif. And during the cooking, a few drops from a tiny bottle season the dish: cocktail bitters.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, natural flavours are extracted by maceration, giving a tincture with colour and broad flavour, or by redistillation, giving a distillate, with vacuum stills for delicate aromas; artificial flavours are cold compounded, and natural colours are unstable. Second, spiced rum is a sweetened golden rum with spices, usually macerated, and flavoured vodka is either traditional and macerated, or modern, with premium versions macerated then redistilled. Third, aniseed spirits get anethole from aniseed, fennel and star anise and louche with water; pastis must contain liquorice and be sweetened, absinthe should contain wormwood and is unsweetened; and bitters come as aperitif, digestif or cocktail bitters.

In this lesson we stand in front of the most colourful shelf of any bar: the liqueurs. There are hundreds of them, in every shade from electric blue to ruby red, and at first they can look impossible to organise. In fact, a few simple ideas are enough. We will see what a liqueur is, which base spirits it can start from, what flavours it can carry, why it is always sweet and often coloured, how its strength differs from other spirits, and how to group liqueurs so that any bottle makes sense.

Let us start with a definition. A liqueur is a flavoured spirit that has been sweetened. That is all, but every word counts. Flavoured means that the flavour is added to a spirit that already exists, using the techniques we met in the previous lesson: maceration, redistillation, or bought-in natural or artificial flavourings. Sweetened is the decisive part: sugar is what separates a liqueur from the other flavoured spirits, like gin or bitters.

Now the base spirit. Most liqueurs are made from neutral spirit. The reason is the same as for gin: a neutral background lets the added flavours shine without competition, like a white plate that shows off the food. Some liqueurs, however, deliberately start from a characterful spirit, and you can taste that spirit in the final drink. There are well-known liqueurs built on Cognac, for example, and others built on Scotch whisky. In these cases the base is not just a carrier but part of the style.

Next, the flavourings. Here there are no limits at all. Some producers concentrate on one flavour, or one type of flavour, such as a single fruit or a single seed. Others use complex recipes with dozens of herbs and spices, and these recipes are often closely guarded secrets. Think of the difference between a single-fruit jam and a spice cake with twenty ingredients: both are sweet, but one tells a simple story and the other a complicated one.

One ingredient deserves a special mention: cream. Using cream in a liqueur is a relatively modern idea, and it is technically demanding. Cream must be handled with complex techniques so that it does not form lumps once the liqueur is in the bottle. The result is unusual in the world of drinks: cream liqueurs are among the very few truly opaque alcoholic beverages. If you hold one up to the light, nothing passes through.

Now sweetness. Every liqueur has added sugar. The legal minimum varies from country to country, but the outcome is always the same: every liqueur is correctly described as sweet. So in a tasting there is no such thing as a dry liqueur. If a flavoured spirit is not sweet, it is simply not a liqueur, but some other kind of flavoured spirit. This is one of the easiest points to score in an exam, so hold on to it.

Colour, on the other hand, is optional, but very common. Liqueurs are often vividly coloured, and artificial colours are widely used. As we saw earlier, natural colour from plants is unstable and can change from bottle to bottle, so many producers support it or replace it with approved food colourings. That explains the emerald greens, electric blues and bright reds on bar shelves, colours that rarely come straight from nature.

Another difference concerns strength. Most spirits have a legal minimum bottling strength: thirty-seven and a half percent alcohol by volume in the European Union, and forty percent in the United States. Liqueurs, however, may be bottled below that. This has a practical consequence behind the bar. Once opened, lower-strength liqueurs lose their freshness faster than strong spirits, so they should be used up sooner and not left open on a shelf for months.

Finally, how to find your way. With so many liqueurs, the most helpful approach is to group them by their main flavour. The four useful groups are: herb; fruit; seed, nut and kernel; and cream. Faced with an unfamiliar bottle, ask yourself which family its dominant flavour belongs to. A herbal liqueur behaves like other herbal liqueurs, a nut liqueur like other nut liqueurs, and so on. This makes it much easier to compare two products and to decide how to use them in a drink.

Here is a memory tip: think of a liqueur as a sweet shop. Every jar on the shelves is sweet, that is the rule of the shop. Most jars are clear glass, the neutral base, but a few are made of finer material, the characterful base. And the shop is arranged in four aisles: herbs, fruit, nuts and seeds, and cream.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, a liqueur is a flavoured spirit that has been sweetened, usually on a neutral base, though some start from a characterful spirit such as Cognac or Scotch whisky. Second, any flavour is allowed, including cream, which needs special techniques and makes some of the few opaque alcoholic drinks; and liqueurs are often vividly coloured, frequently with artificial colours. Third, every liqueur is sweet, liqueurs may be bottled at a lower strength than other spirits, which makes opened bottles fade sooner, and the four flavour groups are herb, fruit, seed, nut and kernel, and cream.

In this lesson we leave spirits for a moment, because our subject is not a spirit at all. Aromatised wines are wines flavoured with botanicals, but they are so important behind the bar that every bartender needs to understand them. The most important of them, by far, is vermouth, because it is the one that cocktails call for most often. We will look at the four ingredients of an aromatised wine, the role of fortification, how everything is blended, what makes a vermouth a vermouth, and where most of it comes from.

Every aromatised wine follows the same basic recipe: a base wine, flavoured with botanicals, with its alcohol raised by adding distilled alcohol, usually sweetened, and sometimes coloured. Let us take these ingredients one by one, as if we were walking through a kitchen where each element is prepared separately before the final assembly.

First, the base wine. Grapes are crushed and their sweet juice is fermented straight away. There are no rules on which grapes can be used, and both white and black grapes are allowed. In practice, though, most producers choose a neutral, high-acid white variety. It gives a dry, discreet base wine that lets the botanicals shine. Think of a plain canvas again: the less the wine says, the more clearly the botanicals can speak.

Here is a surprise that often appears in exams: most red vermouths are not made from red wine. They are made from white wine, coloured with caramel. So when you see a deep red vermouth, picture a white wine that has been tinted, not a red wine that has been flavoured. The colour tells you about the style and the sweetness, not about the grapes.

Second, the botanicals. Producers usually process each botanical separately, using the two techniques we already know: maceration, which gives tinctures, and redistillation, which gives distillates. Some producers take another route and macerate the botanicals directly in the wine. There are no limits on which flavours can be used, recipes are closely guarded secrets, and certain artificial flavourings are also allowed. For vermouth, however, there is one specific requirement, which we will come to shortly.

Third, the distilled alcohol. It must be added to every aromatised wine, raising its strength to between fourteen and a half and twenty-two percent alcohol by volume. This addition is called fortification, which makes these drinks a type of fortified wine. Fortification does three useful jobs. It gives a longer shelf life. It keeps the wine stable. And above all, since most aromatised wines are sweetened, it stops yeast from fermenting the added sugar, because yeast cannot survive at that strength. Most producers use neutral alcohol, so that the spirit adds no flavour that could compete with the botanicals.

Fourth, sugar and colour. Most aromatised wines are sweetened, in varying amounts, and caramel may be added for colour if needed. Then comes blending, at the very end of the process. The dry base wine is mixed with the distilled alcohol, the botanical distillates and tinctures, the sugar and, if required, the caramel. In most cases the blend then rests for a few weeks in stainless steel tanks, so that all the flavours can come together before bottling. Some producers use oak barrels instead, which lets the wine mature and gain extra complexity, a little like a sauce that tastes more harmonious the day after it is made.

Now, what makes a vermouth? Under European law, the defining feature is that plants from the wormwood family must be part of the botanical recipe. You met wormwood with absinthe, as a floral, bitter plant; here it gives vermouth its characteristic bitter edge. Vermouth comes in red or white styles, and at a range of sweetness levels, from dry to sweet. That double choice, colour and sweetness, is exactly what bartenders play with: a dry white vermouth in one classic, a sweet red one in another.

Where is vermouth made? Aromatised wines can be produced anywhere in the world, and with the popularity of cocktails new and inventive versions are appearing in many countries. Even so, the great majority still come from an area that straddles the Alps, taking in south-east France and north-west Italy. Of all the types made there, vermouth is by far the most important.

Here is a memory tip: think of vermouth as a wine wearing a winter coat. The wine underneath is a plain, crisp white. The coat is made of three layers: alcohol to keep it warm and stable, botanicals with a lining of wormwood for character, and sugar for comfort. And if the coat is red, it has simply been dyed with caramel.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, an aromatised wine starts from a dry, neutral, high-acid white wine, even for most red vermouths, which are coloured with caramel. Second, it is flavoured with botanical tinctures and distillates, fortified with usually neutral alcohol to between fourteen and a half and twenty-two percent, which stops yeast fermenting the added sugar, and everything is blended at the end, then rested in steel or sometimes oak. Third, a vermouth must include plants from the wormwood family, comes in red or white and from dry to sweet, and is made mostly in the Alpine area of south-east France and north-west Italy.

In this lesson we step behind the bar. Bartenders are skilled professionals who work fast and with precision, and who are hosts and salespeople at the same time. We cannot teach all of that in one lesson, but we can learn the stage they work on. We will look at how a bar is laid out and how spirits are stored, at the workstation, at the core tools of the trade, and finally at the classic glasses and the drinks they are linked to.

First, the layout. A bar is split into two halves: the bar counter and the back bar, and the bartender works in the space between them. Everything is arranged so that the movements needed to make and serve a drink are few and short. That is not a detail: a well-organised bar is noticeably faster and serves better drinks. A word on storage, too. Unopened spirits should be kept at a cool, constant temperature, away from direct sunlight. Once opened, they slowly react with oxygen and lose freshness, faster for lower-strength liqueurs, and faster for any bottle once it is more than half empty.

The bar counter is divided into individual workstations. Layouts vary, but they share common features. The part the customer sees is the bar top, where drinks are prepared on drip mats that catch spills before they spread. Within easy reach sit a napkin holder, a straw caddy and the most-used tools: shakers, strainers, jiggers and bar spoons.

Right behind the bar top is the heart of the workstation, holding everything needed constantly. There is the ice well, with sections for cubed and crushed ice. Ice must always be handled with a scoop or tongs, never with hands and never by scooping with a glass. There is the speed rail, a low rack holding the house spirits within reach; garnish trays; chilled fresh juices; a soda gun; a chopping board; a bin; and a sink for washing equipment. In the United States, bars must have separate sinks for washing tools and washing hands.

Then the back bar. It is a storage area, but also a shop window. On its counter and shelves the full range of spirits, liqueurs and bitters is displayed to inspire customers and show off the style of the bar. Below the counter is the practical storage: fridges and shelving for wine, beer, soft drinks and glassware.

Now the tools, starting with measuring. The jigger is a calibrated measure, and it is the easiest way to make cocktails consistent and keep them balanced. A bottle pourer, fitted to frequently used bottles, limits the flow and makes it easier to pour accurately into the jigger. The bar spoon has two jobs: measuring small quantities and stirring drinks.

Next, mixing and straining. Shakers come in many styles. A two-piece shaker has two stainless steel halves called tins, or one glass half and one steel half; three-piece shakers exist too. The mixing glass is used for stirred drinks. Each has its partner strainer: the Hawthorne goes with the shaker, the Julep strainer with the mixing glass. With a Hawthorne, the bartender controls the pouring speed by moving the strainer. It is often used together with a fine sieve, which catches small shards of ice. Using both is called double straining.

For garnishes, you need a sharp knife; a peeler for larger pieces of citrus peel; a channel knife for narrow strips; a grater, for nutmeg for example; and a lighter for flamed garnishes. The kit is completed by the muddler, which crushes ingredients such as lime wedges or mint to release juice and aromatic oils; the juicer, essential because juices should always be fresh; the ice scoop for filling shakers and glasses; tongs for placing individual cubes; the bar blade for opening mixers and beers; and the waiter's friend corkscrew for wine.

Now the glasses. The right glass matters because it shapes how the drink looks. For spirits, there is the shot glass, for a single measure drunk in one go, and the balloon, or snifter, whose wide bowl and narrow opening show off oak-aged spirits such as brandy. The tumbler, also called the Old Fashioned glass, serves spirits neat or on the rocks, meaning over ice, and several spirit-forward cocktails, including the one that gave it its name.

For short drinks served without ice, which bartenders call straight up, there is the V-shaped Martini glass, the coupe, once used for Champagne, and the Margarita glass, named after the tequila sour. The Champagne flute is used for the Champagne Cocktail: Cognac, sugar, bitters and Champagne. For long drinks, with a mixer and plenty of ice, the workhorse is the highball, or Collins glass, which also suits soft drinks and beer. The sling is tall and tapered on a short stem, named after the Singapore Sling. The hurricane, pear-shaped like a storm lamp, holds tropical drinks such as the Piña Colada: white rum, pineapple juice and coconut cream.

Some vessels belong to one drink. The Mule mug traditionally serves the Moscow Mule: vodka, ginger beer and lime. The julep cup serves the Mint Julep: Bourbon, mint, sugar and crushed ice. The toddy glass is for hot drinks such as Irish coffee: coffee, Irish whiskey, sugar and cream. And the tiki mug goes with elaborate, mostly rum-based tiki cocktails, part of a flamboyant style loosely inspired by Polynesia.

Here is a memory tip for the strainers: match each one to a movement. The shaker is shaken hard, and the Hawthorne, with its springy coil, keeps up with that energy. The mixing glass is stirred calmly, the way a julep is sipped slowly, so it gets the simple Julep strainer. Shaken drink, Hawthorne; stirred drink, Julep.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, a bar has a counter and a back bar; each workstation has drip mats, an ice well handled only with a scoop or tongs, and a speed rail for the house spirits. Second, the jigger and pourer give accurate measures; the shaker pairs with the Hawthorne, often plus a fine sieve for double straining, and the mixing glass with the Julep strainer. Third, the balloon and tumbler serve spirits; the Martini, coupe and Margarita glasses serve short drinks; the highball, sling and hurricane serve long drinks; and the Mule mug, julep cup, toddy and tiki mug each have their own drinks.

In this lesson we look at what goes into a cocktail besides the spirit, and at the principle that holds everything together: balance. Cocktails are the only drinks made at the moment of service, so the bartender is both the cook and the waiter. We will cover five key ingredients, ice, simple and flavoured syrups, fruit juices, cocktail bitters and garnishes, and then the two sets of scales a bartender uses to make sure every drink is balanced.

Let us start with the ingredient people forget: ice. Ice has two jobs. The first, and the most important, is to chill the drink, either while it is being made or once it is served. The second is to help with dilution, adding a little water as it melts. To do both jobs well, ice must be very cold and dry. Ice that is close to zero degrees Celsius chills poorly and melts too fast, so the drink ends up watery.

Bars use many types of ice, but two matter most: cubed and crushed. Cubed ice is used to make both shaken and stirred drinks. Shaking with cubes chills a drink quickly and dilutes it slightly. Stirring chills more slowly, so the dilution can be greater than in a shaken drink. Once it has been used to prepare a drink, that ice is thrown away. When cubes are served in the glass, their job is to chill, not to dilute. That is why long drinks such as a gin and tonic or a Cuba Libre should be served in a glass full of ice.

This sounds wrong at first: surely more ice means more water? In fact the opposite is true. With a glass full of ice, the ratio of ice to liquid is high, so the drink stays cold and the ice melts slowly. With just a few cubes floating in a lot of liquid, the ice melts quickly and waters the drink down. Crushed ice is different: it is meant to chill and dilute fast, and it gives drinks such as the Mojito and the Caipirinha their typical frosty look.

Next, sweetness. Simple syrups are the preferred way to sweeten a cocktail, because a ready-made liquid makes accurate measuring easy. Many bars make their own. A common recipe is two parts sugar to one part water. Some bartenders prefer this two-to-one syrup to a one-to-one syrup because it delivers the same sweetness in less volume, leaving more room in the glass for characterful ingredients. Syrups can also be flavoured, which adds complexity. A classic example is orgeat, a syrup flavoured with almond and rose water or orange flower water.

Then the fruit juices. The best bartenders use only freshly squeezed citrus juice. It oxidises and loses freshness quickly, so it must be kept chilled, and even then it can deteriorate within hours. In the best bars, juice is squeezed in batches as needed, sometimes several times a night. Other juices, such as cranberry, are usually bought ready-made. Cocktail bitters are extremely bitter flavoured spirits, usually with pronounced aromas too. They are a seasoning, never a main ingredient: a few dashes add an extra dimension, like salt and pepper on a dish.

Finally, garnishes. Their first job is to decorate the drink, and they should improve its look, not spoil it. They often add a subtle aroma that accentuates or complements one already in the drink. Common garnishes include lemon and lime wedges, mint, olives and maraschino cherries. Fresh fruit garnishes should be cut on the day and thrown away at the end of the night; mint must be handled gently so it does not wilt or bruise. Preserved olives and cherries are less delicate, but still need proper storage.

Now the heart of the lesson: balance. Every good bartender aims for a balanced drink, and there are two sets of scales to help. The first sets strong against weak. Strong is the alcoholic part of the drink. Weak is the non-alcoholic liquid: fruit juice, soda water, tonic water. This is the great advantage of a cocktail: you enjoy the flavours of a spirit without its full strength.

Remember that ice belongs on the weak side as well. Some of it melts while the drink is being shaken or stirred, and that water lengthens the drink. In some cocktails, such as the Martini, melted ice is actually the main weak element. So the time spent stirring or shaking is not a detail: it decides how much water ends up in the glass, and therefore how strong the drink tastes.

The second set of scales puts sweet on one side and sour and, or, bitter on the other. Sweetness can come from sugar, a simple syrup or a liqueur. But a drink that is only sweet is not balanced. It needs a counterweight: a sour ingredient, such as citrus juice, or a bitter one, most obviously cocktail bitters. Vermouth is special, because it brings both sweetness and bitterness at once.

Put the two scales together and you have the formula behind most cocktails: a strong part, a weak part, a sweet ingredient, and a sour or bitter one. There are always exceptions, but this rule explains why the classics work, and it helps you fix a drink. If a cocktail tastes cloying, add a touch of citrus. If the alcohol burns, it needs more of the weak side.

Here is a memory tip: picture a bartender holding two pairs of old-fashioned kitchen scales. On the first, a bottle of spirit sits opposite a jug of juice and a bucket of melting ice. On the second, a pot of syrup sits opposite a lemon and a tiny bottle of bitters. A balanced drink is one where both scales are level.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, ice must be cold and dry; it chills first and dilutes second; serve long drinks in a glass full of cubes, and use crushed ice to chill and dilute fast. Second, two-to-one simple syrup gives sweetness in less volume, orgeat is a flavoured syrup, citrus juice must be fresh and made in batches, bitters are a seasoning, and fresh garnishes are cut daily. Third, balance means strong against weak, where meltwater counts as weak, and sweet against sour or bitter, with vermouth bringing both sweet and bitter.

In this lesson we meet the great cocktail families. There are hundreds of classics, and the list can feel endless, but it is far less chaotic than it looks. Every cocktail is built from the four points of balance: strong, weak, sour or bitter, and sweet. Take a balanced recipe, swap one ingredient, and a new drink is born. That is how families form. We will look at the main preparation methods, then at five families: highball, sour, Collins, punch and spirit-forward.

First, the methods. A bartender wants to do two things: chill the drink and mix the ingredients thoroughly. Building is the simplest method: the ingredients are poured straight into a glass filled with cubed ice, usually up to about one centimetre from the rim. Stirring means putting the ingredients in a mixing glass with cubed ice, stirring with a bar spoon until the right level of chilling and dilution is reached, then straining with a Julep strainer into a prepared glass.

Shaking means putting the ingredients and cubed ice into one half of a shaker, sealing it firmly with the other half, and shaking hard. This mixes and chills, but it also adds air, giving shaken drinks a lighter, frothier texture than stirred ones. Shaking can break the ice, so the drink is strained through a Hawthorne strainer and usually a fine sieve as well: double straining. Two more techniques complete the toolkit. Muddling crushes fruit or herbs, such as lime or mint, to release juice and aroma, gently, because delicate ingredients are easily overworked. Blending whizzes ingredients with crushed ice to give a notably smooth texture.

Now the families, starting with the simplest of all mixed drinks: the highball. It is a spirit, the strong part, lengthened with a mixer, juice or soda, the weak part, and served long over cubed ice. Think of gin and tonic, vodka and tonic, or whisky and soda. Sometimes a sour or bitter touch is added: a squeeze of citrus or a few dashes of bitters. The method is building, straight into the glass.

Some highballs have their own names. The Cuba Libre is rum and cola with lime. The Moscow Mule is vodka topped with ginger beer and lime, traditionally served in its copper Mule mug. And the Horse's Neck combines whisky, ginger ale and bitters, showing that a highball can carry a bitter element too.

The second family is the sour, built on the classic balance of strong, sour and sweet: a spirit, fresh lemon or lime juice, and a sweetener such as simple syrup. Sours are shaken over ice and strained. Classic sours use an unflavoured sweetener. The Whisky Sour uses Bourbon or rye, lemon juice and simple syrup, with egg white as an option. The Pisco Sour uses pisco, lime juice, simple syrup and an egg white, which is essential here, because egg white gives a smooth, mouthfilling texture. The Daiquiri is white rum, lime juice and syrup. Tommy's Margarita is tequila, lime juice and agave syrup.

More complex sours change the sweetener or the sour element. Swap the syrup for triple sec, an orange liqueur, and you get a new set of classics, because triple sec brings both sweetness and orange aroma. The Sidecar is Cognac, lemon juice and triple sec. The Margarita is tequila, lime juice and triple sec, often with a salt rim. And the Cosmopolitan goes one step further: vodka, triple sec, and two sour or fruity elements, lime juice and cranberry juice. Line them up and the family logic is clear: one structure, a couple of swaps, completely different drinks.

The third family is the Collins, which you can think of as a sour turned into a long drink. It combines a spirit, lemon or lime juice and a sweetener, topped up with soda water and served over cubed ice. It can be made two ways: shake the spirit, juice and syrup and then top with soda, or build everything in the glass over ice. The classic is the Tom Collins: gin, lemon juice, simple syrup and soda. Change only the spirit and the variations appear: vodka for a Vodka Collins, Cognac for a Pierre Collins, rum for a Pedro Collins.

Other members add extra ingredients. The Mojito uses rum, lime juice, sugar or syrup, mint leaves and soda water, and unlike the others it is served over crushed ice. The Paloma uses tequila and lime juice with a Mexican grapefruit soda, or with grapefruit juice and soda water. Close to the Collins is the punch, which has a long and complicated history. Punches also have a sour base, but they use juices, often tropical, instead of soda, and add bitters or spices. Today they are mainly linked to rum, and can be served as a sharing drink, in a large bowl from which guests help themselves with a ladle.

The fifth family is the spirit-forward cocktail. These drinks are higher in alcohol and celebrate their main spirit. Sweetness and bitterness are balanced with combinations of sugar, vermouth and bitters. They are stirred over cubed ice, and here stirring is critical, because the ice controls the dilution. They are then strained and served straight up or over ice. The Manhattan and the Martini use vermouth. The Old Fashioned, whisky with sugar and bitters, gave its name to the tumbler; the Sazerac also uses sugar and bitters, on rye or Cognac. The Negroni, a close relative, combines equal parts gin, red vermouth and an aperitif bitter, served over ice.

Customers often have strong views on their Martini. Less vermouth makes it drier, more vermouth makes it wetter, and a little olive brine makes it dirty. The garnish matters more here than in almost any other drink: a lemon or grapefruit twist, or olives. The classic Manhattan is rye, sweet vermouth and bitters. Add a spoon of maraschino syrup for a Sweet Manhattan, use dry vermouth for a Dry Manhattan, or equal parts dry and sweet for a Perfect Manhattan. Bourbon can replace the rye; with Irish whiskey the drink becomes an Emerald, and with Scotch whisky a Rob Roy.

Here is a memory tip: think of the families as a growing house. The highball is a single room: spirit and mixer. Add lemon and sugar and shake, and you have the sour. Add a soda roof on top of the sour, and you have the Collins. Swap the roof for tropical juice and spices, and you have the punch. And the spirit-forward cocktail is the cellar: no juice, no soda, just spirit, vermouth or sugar, and bitters, stirred slowly.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, the methods: build in the glass over ice, stir in a mixing glass and strain with a Julep, shake and double strain with a Hawthorne and fine sieve, muddle gently, blend with crushed ice. Second, the highball is spirit plus mixer, like the Cuba Libre and Moscow Mule; the sour is spirit, citrus and sweetener, with triple sec in the Sidecar, Margarita and Cosmopolitan; the Collins is a sour with soda, like the Tom Collins, Mojito and Paloma. Third, spirit-forward drinks are stirred and balanced with vermouth or sugar and bitters: Manhattan, Martini, Old Fashioned, Sazerac, Negroni.

In this final lesson we learn how to taste a spirit like a professional. Tasting, rather than simply drinking, means examining a spirit step by step so that you can describe it to someone else, sometimes weeks later. That matters to anyone who makes, sells or mixes spirits. We will cover tasting conditions, the four steps of appearance, nose, palate and finish, the three sources of aromas, and how to judge quality.

First, preparation. Nothing outside the glass should change your impression. The ideal room is free of smells, such as cleaning products, smoke, food or perfume, with good natural light and white surfaces for judging colour. Your palate should be clean, so avoid coffee, gum or toothpaste just before; a piece of bread helps clear lingering flavours. Colds, hay fever and tiredness dull your senses and your judgement.

Next, the glass. To compare spirits fairly, use one type of glass for every sample. The ideal glass has a rounded bowl large enough to take some water, sides that curve inwards like a tulip to concentrate the aromas, and a stem, so your hand does not warm the liquid. A small sample is enough: about one and a half centilitres.

Now step one: appearance, observed before adding any water. Note the clarity, the intensity of colour and the colour itself. Be aware that colour tells you little about quality or age. Every spirit comes off the still as clear as water; any colour comes later, from oak, caramel or botanicals, and filtration can remove it. Most spirits are clear, and haze is usually a fault, although some unfiltered premium spirits turn slightly hazy when chilled or diluted. Aniseed spirits go cloudy when water is added: that is louching.

Step two: the nose. Bring the glass gently to your nose and take short, quick sniffs. Do not swirl as you would with wine: swirling a spirit releases so much alcohol that it numbs your sense of smell. First ask: is it clean? A strong smell of solvent means the distiller kept too much of the heads. Plastic, cheese or sweat point to too much of the tails. A musty, damp cardboard smell means cork taint. These faults are rare. The commonest is more ordinary: a bottle open too long, which smells tired and less fresh.

Then judge the intensity. Most spirits are light, medium or pronounced. Vodka is the exception: its makers aim for such a light intensity that it is described as neutral, which does not mean it has no aroma at all. After nosing the spirit neat, add an equal volume of water, a fifty-fifty mix, and smell again. Water opens up the aromas, reveals hidden layers and makes it easier to tell one aroma from another. Always dilute the same way, or your comparisons will mean nothing. Some tasters leave certain fruit spirits undiluted, finding that water blurs their aromas.

Step three: the palate. Take a small sip of the diluted sample, spread it all around your mouth, and hold it for a few seconds. Neat spirit would numb your mouth. The tongue recognises sweet, sour, salt, bitter and umami, but with spirits sweetness and bitterness are what count. Sweetness is judged on a scale, and it measures sugar added after distillation. A freshly distilled spirit is dry. Many Cognacs are off-dry, many rums medium, and liqueurs and pastis sweet. Beware the illusion: vanilla and fruity aromas can seem sweet without any sugar. Texture helps here, because added sugar feels thicker, a little syrupy.

Texture is described in words rather than on a scale. Ask yourself: does the spirit feel rough or smooth and silky? Is it warming, full and mouthfilling, or watery and thin? Then come the flavours. Flavours usually mirror the aromas, because they reach your nose from the back of the mouth. Finally, the finish. After you spit or swallow, draw a little air over your tongue and notice how long the pleasant flavours last, ignoring any unpleasant ones, and whether one simple flavour dominates or many complex ones unfold.

Now, where do aromas come from? Describing aromas is subjective, but some notes have clear explanations, and experienced tasters use them consistently. To bring order, sort each aroma into one of three sources. The first is the raw material. Corn gives butterscotch, popcorn and sweetcorn. Malted barley gives porridge, cereal and flour. Rye gives rye bread and peppery spice. Grapes give dried fruit like fig, prune and raisin, or flowers. Agave gives vegetal, root and olive notes. Sugar cane gives grass, molasses and burnt sugar. In flavoured spirits, the botanicals dominate: juniper, aniseed, cinnamon and herbs.

The second source is processing. Peat and roasting bring smoke, medicinal, smoked fish or seaweed notes. Fermentation creates fruity esters such as banana, pear, pineapple, pear drops and even nail varnish. Heads and tails belong here too: in small amounts they add character, in excess they become faults like prickly solvent or burnt rubber. The third source is oak and maturation. Oak can be obvious, with vanilla, coconut, toast, coffee or sweet spice, or discreet, just a gentle spiciness. Long ageing with some oxygen adds fruit cake, candied fruit, leather, tobacco, forest floor, mushroom and wood polish. Train your memory with real fruit and spices, and use words others understand.

Finally, quality. Judging quality is not the same as saying whether you like a spirit. You may dislike peat and still recognise an excellent peated whisky. Measure the spirit against shared criteria and its own style. The first criterion is balance: if one element, such as alcohol heat, flattens everything else, the spirit is unbalanced. Balance can come from every part being moderate, or from one star that does not smother the rest. Then the finish: complex, pleasant flavours that linger and evolve point to high quality. Then expressiveness, how clearly the spirit speaks of its raw material, processing or oak. For vodka, look instead for purity: a smooth, seamless texture carrying delicate flavours.

Put together, these lead to a verdict on a scale from faulty, through poor and acceptable, to good, very good and outstanding. A balanced spirit with distinctive features for its style is good. One lacking character or balance drops to acceptable or poor. Particularly fine balance, or an extra layer of complexity and expressiveness, especially on the finish, makes it very good. All of this at the highest level: outstanding.

Here is a memory tip for the whole method, five short verbs: look, sniff, sip, wait, judge. Look before water. Sniff in short breaths, never swirl. Sip after water. Wait for the finish to fade. Judge with your head, not your heart.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, taste in an odour-free, well-lit room, with one stemmed tulip glass for all and an equal volume of water after the first look and sniff. Second, colour says little; solvent means heads, plastic or cheese means tails, damp cardboard means cork; sweetness measures added sugar, and the finish counts only pleasant flavours. Third, aromas come from the raw material, processing, or oak and maturation, and quality is judged on balance, finish, expressiveness or, for vodka, purity, from faulty to outstanding.
